# Introduction

Everything in NYTE City has a price. That's not philosophy — it's the operating principle of the place. The clothes on your back, the roof over your head, the piece on your hip: all of it costs something, and none of it lasts forever. They say the right gear makes the right impression — even if that impression is your knuckle dusters in some ganger's ribs.

This is the only equipment chapter in the book, and it covers everything. Weapons, armor, cybernetics, vehicles, and the miscellaneous hardware that fills the space between — this is where you outfit your character from the ground up, whether that means picking up a Cheapshot at a grey-market kiosk or getting fitted for custom cyberware at your local chopshop. Five categories, one chapter, everything you need to survive another night in NYTE City.

Prices reflect street value — what you'd pay through a legitimate vendor or a reliable fixer without active heat on the transaction. Black market, faction surplus, and stolen hardware may run cheaper or harder to source, depending on your connections and the GM's read of the current climate.

Not everything here is available to everyone. Availability ratings tell you how hard something is to locate; your Streetwise skill and your contacts determine whether "Rare" is a real obstacle or just a Tuesday. The five categories covered in this chapter are:

- **Weapons & Ammunition** — Everything from a big stick to a small cannon that you can use to stay ahead of the rest.

- **Armor** — A physical barrier between you and the thing that wants to kill you.

- **Cybernetics** — Chips, mods, implants, and the other modifications you can make to your body.

- **Equipment** — Crowbars, SMARTdecks, Silver Cards, and everything else that fills the gap between a weapon and a plan.

- **Vehicles** — Whether they run, roll, hover or fly, this is how you get where you're going and how fast you get there when things go wrong.

## Economics in NYTE City

NYTE City runs on two economies operating in parallel, and knowing which one you're in tells you as much about a transaction as the price itself.

**Çredits (Ç)** are the digital currency of the legitimate economy — corporate payroll, licensed vendors, government transactions, anything that goes through the LINK's financial infrastructure. Çredits are tracked. Every purchase leaves a record: who bought what, from whom, when, and where. For most of NYTE City's population this is unremarkable background noise. For operators who prefer their movements unrecorded, it is a persistent liability.

**Skrip (\$)** is physical currency — untraceable by design, equivalent in value to Çredits, and the preferred medium of exchange for anyone conducting business they'd rather not see logged. Under the table work, black market vendors, fixers, and anyone operating in the city's gray economy transacts in skrip. The bills themselves are unremarkable; what they represent is a transaction that doesn't exist as far as any system is concerned.

The two currencies trade at rough parity — 1\$ buys what 1Ç buys. The difference is friction. Vendors who accept skrip occasionally offer a modest discount: no processing fees, no tax record, no oversight cost. The savings get passed on, quietly, to buyers who know to ask.

All prices in this chapter are listed in Çredits (Ç) — the standard of the licensed market. Operators dealing in skrip pay the same price unless the vendor offers otherwise, which some do and some don't, and which is rarely advertised.

### The TAG

Every resident of NYTE City has a **TAG** — a Trusted Authentication Gateway, the government-issued digital identity that connects a person to the city's services, financial infrastructure, and communications network. Your TAG is how people reach you, how vendors charge you, and how you access everything from transit passes to your building's front door. Corporate TAGs, social media TAGs, gaming network TAGs — the term has bled into everyday language the same way "username" did a century earlier.

The TAG system was introduced alongside sweeping automation that displaced millions of workers across manufacturing, logistics, and service industries. The city's response was a **Universal Basic Income** program: every registered resident with a TAG receives **625Ç monthly**, unconditionally. It covers the basics — housing, food, utilities. For residents whose livelihoods were restructured out of existence by AI and robotics, it has been a genuine lifeline.

The tradeoff is visibility. A TAG means the city knows where you are, what you buy, and who you talk to. Most residents accept this as the cost of participation, many don’t. Those who prefer to live without that layer of oversight go **TAGless** — carrying no government identity, operating entirely in the skrip economy, and forgoing the UBI in exchange for living off the grid. It is a legitimate choice, and it comes with real limitations and real freedoms, depending on what you value.

For operators working outside the formal economy — TAGless or otherwise — the Contract Retrieval and Networking Knowledgebase, known on the street as CRANK, is the gray market's answer to corporate employment. Anonymous job postings, reputation-based matching, skrip transactions. The full CRANK system is detailed in Part VI of the GM Workshop, but its function is simple: it connects people with skills to people with problems, no TAG required.

Those running a **Black TAG** have a third option: a false identity that looks legitimate from the outside. The city has systems to detect them. Those systems are imperfect.

### The Economy at a Glance

What does a Çredit actually buy? The table below anchors the currency to daily life in NYTE City. Prices vary by district, vendor, and circumstance — these are baselines, not guarantees.

| Class | Monthly Income | Daily Budget | What That Buys |
|----|----|----|----|
| Underclass | 625Ç (UBI) | 21Ç | A coffin box, fast food, and not much else |
| Working | 2,500Ç | 83Ç | Rent, food, transport — the basics, covered |
| Middle | 5,000Ç | 167Ç | Comfort, discretionary spending, some savings |
| Upper | 12,500Ç | 417Ç | Luxury, investment, significant purchasing power |
| Hyper | 25,000Ç | 833Ç | Whatever they want |

A Working class character earning 2,500Ç/month has roughly one month's income to spend on a Kevlar Vest (500Ç). The BDF Oni heavy pistol at 7,500Ç is three months of saving. Powered Armor and Mechs are out of reach for anyone without significant connections.

# Weapons

### Reading the Tables

Every weapon entry uses the same columns relevant to its type. Here's what each one means.

**Skill** — Which combat skill governs this weapon. You can pick up anything, but you'll feel the difference without the training behind it.

**DMG** — Base damage per hit for each successful hit, before modifiers.

**Style** — The fighting style the weapon is built around: Blade or Blunt. Style determines which conditions a weapon can inflict and how it interacts with armor.

**Reach** — How far the weapon extends from the wielder. A weapon with greater Reach can strike before a shorter weapon can respond.

**Parry** — The defensive bonus the weapon provides when used to block an incoming attack. A weapon with Parry +2 is meaningfully easier to defend with than one with no bonus at all.

**Dam Type** — The damage type the weapon delivers: Normal, Electric, or Energy. Damage type determines what conditions a hit can inflict and how it interacts with armor resistance.

**ACC** — Accuracy bonus applied to attack rolls made at single-shot rate of fire. Burst and full-auto fire do not benefit from Accuracy bonuses.

**Range** — Effective range band. Attacks made beyond this range suffer penalties to both accuracy and damage.

**RoF** — Rate of Fire. Available firing modes: **S** = Single shot, **B** = Burst (3 rounds), **F** = Full Auto (10+ rounds).

**Capacity** — Magazine or power cell size. The number after **+1** represents a chambered round.

**Mods** — Available modification slots. Each slot holds one weapon attachment.

**Availability** — How easy the weapon is to source.

- **Common** means any licensed dealer.

- **Uncommon** requires a specialty vendor or moderate connections.

- **Rare** means permits, serious credits, or a fixer with the right relationships.

- **Exotic** is military, prototype, or off the legal market entirely.

- **By Contract** means the item is not purchased through standard channels — it requires a relationship, not a budget.

**Cost** — Street value in Çredits (Ç). Assumes a clean transaction with no active complications.

**Tags** — Mechanical properties of the weapon: AP, Suppressed, Volatile, Spread, Stunning, Burning, and others.

**Features** — Factory-installed enhancements: SMART Link, Suppressor, Scope, Conceal, and others. These come with the weapon at purchase and are not mod slot upgrades.

#### Damage Types

Damage type describes what the harm actually is — the physics and chemistry of the hit. Types determine which conditions a weapon can inflict and how armor interacts with the damage. Most hits in regular combat do not apply conditions; conditions emerge from critical hits, called shots, specific weapon tags, and circumstances where the fiction demands it.

**Blunt** — Impact force: fists, clubs, bludgeons, pressure waves. Can cause *Stunned* and *Disoriented*. At extremes, *Unconscious*.

**Blade** — Cutting and piercing: knives, swords, claws, monomolecular edges. Can cause *Bleeding*. Precision strikes risk deeper tissue damage.

**Ballistic** — High-velocity projectiles: firearms of all categories. Can cause *Bleeding*, similar to Blade at range. Standard ballistic fire does not risk Maimed or Injured — that threshold belongs to Massive.

**Electric** — Conducted or directed electrical charge: shock weapons, charge cells, taser discharge. Can cause *Stunned/Shocked* and *Paralyzed*. Against targets with significant cyberware, Electric damage may disrupt integrated systems beyond the physical hit — treat as an EMP interaction at the GM's discretion.

**Energy** — Directed energy discharge: lasers, plasma, particle beams. Can cause *Agonized*. Energy wounds are burns and disfigurements — they hurt at a different register than impact or blade wounds, and the pain compounds any subsequent action.

**Burning** — Sustained fire damage: flamethrowers, incendiary rounds, plasma bleed. Always causes *Agonized* and applies ongoing damage each round until the fire is extinguished or the source is removed. Burning stacks with Energy damage when both are present.

#### Damage Categories

**Regular** — The baseline. Blunt force, blade wounds, gunshots, burns — the city's everyday violence. Regular damage can be healed naturally over time or supernaturally, depending on what the target is capable of. Most combat damage is Regular.

**Withering** — The same damage amount as Regular, but delivered through materials and methods specifically harmful to supernatural physiology: silver, cold iron, ultraviolet light, consecrated substances. Withering damage cannot be regenerated supernaturally. A werewolf hit by a silver-tipped arrow heals that wound the slow way — the human way — regardless of what their body would otherwise allow. The damage is not greater. The permanence is. *(Full Withering rules in the Combat chapter.)*

**Massive** — Damage from siege weapons, vehicle-mounted armaments, large-scale explosives, and weapons operating outside the normal envelope of personal combat. Against hard targets — vehicles, mechs, fortifications — Massive damage functions as Regular. Against everything else, it deals double. Massive damage also makes the Maimed and Injured conditions available, representing the kind of force that doesn't just hurt a person — it changes the shape of them. These conditions are not routine outcomes. When they appear, the table will remember.

#### Conditions

Conditions are temporary game states imposed by weapons, substances, and environment. A condition doesn't stack with itself — you either have it or you don't.

Full condition rules, recovery mechanics, and interactions are covered in the **Combat** chapter.

|  |  |  |
|:--:|----|----|
| **Condition** | **Effect** | **Recovery** |
| **Bleeding** | −1 HP per round | BOD Essence TN8 TH1, First Aid, or Nanomed Kit |
| **Burning** | Ongoing damage, −1 to all rolls | Extinguish source, then treat as Bleeding |
| **Disoriented** | −2 to all rolls | BOD Essence TN8 TH1, or end of scene |
| **Stunned** | Can't act, can't move | BOD Essence TN8 TH2 each round |
| **Agonized** | All current penalties doubled | Source removed, or Nanomed Kit |
| **Prone** | Movement halved, attack penalties | Action to stand |
| **Poisoned** | Inflicts Disoriented, Stunned, or Agonized — determined by poison type. Secondary condition cannot clear until poison is removed. | BOD Essence TN8 TH2–4, antidote, or Nanomed Kit |

#### Weapon Tags

Tags are mechanical properties of a weapon that modify how it functions in play. They appear in the Tags column of every weapon table. A tag is not flavor — it has a rule attached to it. When a tag appears, that rule applies.

Tags on ammunition work the same way. A weapon loaded with AP rounds gains the AP tag for those shots. A weapon loaded with standard ammunition does not.

**AP** — Armor Piercing. The weapon or round bypasses the target's RES entirely. PROT still rolls — AP does not make armor irrelevant; it makes the flat damage reduction irrelevant.

**Area (Xm)** — The weapon affects all targets within X meters of the point of impact rather than a single target. The attacker makes one attack roll; all targets in range are affected. Area weapons do not benefit from ACC bonuses — you are covering ground, not aiming precisely. The radius is listed in the tag: Area (5m), Area (10m), etc.

**Bleeding** — The weapon causes the Bleeding condition on a successful hit.

**Burning** — The weapon sets the target on fire. The target takes ongoing damage each round until the fire is extinguished or the source is removed. Burning stacks with Energy damage when both are present.

**Conceal** — The weapon can be concealed on the person without detection by visual inspection or standard security checks. Specialized scanning or a successful Perception check against a defined threshold may reveal it.

**Concussive** — The weapon causes the Disoriented condition across its area of effect. Does not deal damage — the effect is purely the condition. Affects all targets in range including allies.

**Disarming** — This weapon can be used to perform a Disarm combat maneuver instead of dealing damage. Declare Disarm before the attack roll. On a hit, the target's weapon is knocked free. Automatic — no save. The attacker chooses between dealing damage or disarming; they cannot do both on the same hit.

**Disintegration** — On a killing blow, the target leaves no recoverable remains. Nothing to identify, nothing to salvage, nothing to bury. The damage itself is not necessarily greater — the permanence of the outcome is.

**EMP** — The weapon disrupts electronic systems and cybernetic implants on hit. Against standard targets, EMP damage is minimal. Against heavily augmented targets or electronic systems, the EMP effect triggers separately from the damage — cybernetics may shut down, electronic locks may open, vehicles may lose system function.

**Incendiary** — The weapon sets the impact area on fire, causing the Burning condition to all targets in the affected zone. The fire persists until extinguished.

**Knockdown** — This weapon can be used to knock a target prone instead of dealing damage. Declare Knockdown before the attack roll. On a hit, the target is knocked down. Automatic — no save. The attacker chooses between dealing damage or knocking down; they cannot do both on the same hit.

**Mounted** — This weapon requires a bipod, hardpoint, or vehicle mount for effective use. Firing without a mount: make a BOD Essence Check before firing. On success, fire normally at −4 ACC. On failure, the weapon is uncontrollable — the GM determines who in the arc takes the hit, friend or foe.

**No Recoil** — This weapon produces no recoil on discharge. ACC bonus applies to both Single and Burst fire modes. Standard weapons only benefit from ACC on Single fire.

**Non-lethal** — This weapon is designed for incapacitation rather than harm. Descriptor only — the weapon's damage value (or lack thereof) determines the mechanical effect.

**Payload** — The weapon's effect is determined by the equipped arrowhead or bolt type rather than the platform itself.

**Siege** — This weapon deals Massive damage. Against hardened targets — vehicles, structures, fortifications, mech suits — Siege weapons deal regular damage. Against soft targets — people, unarmored personnel — Siege weapons deal double damage. Most personal armor was not designed with Siege weapons in mind.

**Silent** — This weapon produces no ballistic or acoustic signature detectable by standard means. When firing from a hidden position, the attacker is not automatically revealed by the shot. The ambush bonus applies each round the attacker remains undetected rather than only on the first round. Targets may still attempt to locate the shooter through movement, Combat Sense checks, or line of sight — the shot itself does not give them away.

**Smoke** — The weapon creates an obscurement cloud that blocks line of sight within its area. Targets inside the cloud cannot be seen from outside; targets outside cannot be seen from inside. The cloud persists for a number of rounds determined by the GM based on environmental conditions.

**Spread** — The weapon discharges across a cone rather than at a single target, affecting multiple targets simultaneously. Treated as an Area attack — the attacker makes one roll against the group. ACC bonus does not apply. The cone's extent is determined by the weapon's effective range.

**Stunning** — The weapon causes the Stunned/Shocked condition on a successful hit.

**UV Burst (Undead)** — The weapon emits a burst of ultraviolet radiation that deals Withering damage specifically to undead and vampiric targets. Non-supernatural targets in range are unaffected by the UV component.

**Unstable** — This weapon does not behave predictably. Roll 1d4 when used to determine the actual effect.

**Volatile** — This weapon's experimental or hybrid systems carry a risk of malfunction. On a botched attack roll, roll on the Volatile Misfire table.

##### *Volatile Misfire Table (1d4):*

| Roll | Result |
|:--:|----|
| 1 | **No Effect** — The shot goes wide. The weapon functions normally. |
| 2–3 | **Jam** — The weapon cannot fire until cleared. Clearing takes one Action. |
| 4 | **Misfire** — The weapon discharges in hand. Take 5 damage, ignoring armor. The weapon then jams and must be cleared. |

**Wither Cloud (Lycanthropes)** — The weapon creates a zone of particulate matter that converts all damage dealt to lycanthropes and their kindred within the area into Withering damage for the duration. Non-supernatural targets inside the cloud are unaffected by the cloud itself.

**Withering** — Damage of this type cannot be regenerated supernaturally. Vampires, werewolves, and other supernatural entities with regenerative capabilities must heal Withering damage through natural healing only, regardless of their normal recovery rate. The damage amount is not necessarily greater — the permanence is.

#### Weapon Features

Features are factory-installed enhancements that come with specific weapons at purchase. Unlike Tags, Features are properties of the manufacturing rather than the weapon's mechanical function in combat. They appear in the Features column of ranged weapon tables.

**Bipod Mount** — The weapon includes an integrated bipod for stable firing from a prone or braced position. Satisfies the Mounted tag requirement without needing a separate mount.

**Conceal** — As a factory feature rather than a tag, this indicates the weapon was specifically engineered for concealment — slim profile, reduced signature, designed to pass visual inspection. Distinct from a weapon that happens to be small enough to hide.

**Scope** — The weapon includes a factory-fitted precision optic. Provides targeting assistance at long range. Specific mechanical bonus defined by the scope type installed.

**SMART Link** — The weapon integrates with the SMART Link neural interface. Operators with a SMART Link implant gain the full targeting benefit. Operators without one gain no bonus from this feature.

**Suppressor** — The weapon includes a factory-fitted suppressor, granting the Silent tag. Distinct from the Silencer mod, which is an aftermarket attachment. Factory suppressors are purpose-built for the specific weapon and generally more effective than aftermarket alternatives.

**Vehicle Mount** — The weapon requires a vehicle hardpoint or dedicated mount system. Satisfies the Mounted tag requirement only when properly installed on a compatible vehicle.

#### Weapon Modifications

Weapons with available mod slots can be customized through attachments and modifications. Each modification occupies one or more slots. Modifications can be installed by any competent gunsmith or armorer; the Angel Mod requires a specialist. Removing a modification frees the slot but may damage the modification itself depending on what was installed.

The number of mod slots on a weapon is fixed at purchase. Slots cannot be added after manufacture.

| Mod | Slots | Effect |
|:--:|----|----|
| Silencer | 1 | Grants the Silent tag. Subsonic fire only — cannot be applied to shotguns or heavy weapons. Requires subsonic ammunition. Anyone within 6m may make a Combat Sense check to locate the source. |
| Laser Sight | 1 | +1 ACC on aimed shots, stacking with other accuracy bonuses. Green lasers can cause Disoriented on direct unprotected eye contact. |
| Holo Sight | 1 | +1 ACC on aimed shots, stacking with other accuracy bonuses. Does not stack with SMART Targeting. Displays magazine count in the sight picture. |
| Scope | 1 | +2 ACC on aimed shots at Long or Extreme range only. No benefit at Medium range or closer. Does not stack with Holo Sight or Laser Sight. Compatible with rifles and the ADS TC-1 Strix only. |
| Flashlight | 1 | Eliminates darkness penalties for shooting and movement. Active light reveals position — cannot hide in darkness while the light is on. |
| Biometrics | 2 | Registers the weapon to a single authorized user via biometric data at installation. Any other operator attempting to fire the weapon cannot do so. |
| Angel Mod | 2 | Plasma-coated projectile system requiring a powered magazine and Angel Rounds. Grants +4 DMG, AP, Burning, and Agonized on every hit. On a botched attack roll, roll 1d100 — 50 or below the weapon jams; 51 or above the weapon is destroyed. Ammunition, cleaning, and magazine costs are 5× standard. Requires specialist installation. |

**Silencer** — A fitted suppressor for subsonic fire, installed for weapons that don't come with one factory-built. Less effective than a purpose-built factory suppressor but functional — the shot doesn't announce itself at range, and anyone close enough to hear it still has to find where it came from.

**Laser Sight** — A red or green laser mounted under the muzzle or alongside it. The dot doesn't lie. Green lasers carry an additional risk for unprotected eyes at close range — direct contact causes Disoriented.

**Holo Sight** — A holographic sight projecting a reticle visible to the naked eye, with a heads-up magazine count overlaid at the bottom of the display. Faster acquisition than iron sights, more intuitive than a scope at close-to-medium range. Doesn't play well with SMART Targeting — the two systems read the same data differently and interfere with each other.

**Scope** — Magnified optics for precision work at distance. The +2 ACC applies only when the target is at Long or Extreme range — at closer distances the magnification narrows the field of view to the point where it's a liability rather than an advantage. Mounting a scope doesn't make a weapon a sniper rifle. It makes it better at what it was already doing at range. Compatible with rifles and the ADS TC-1 Strix.

**Flashlight** — A tactical light mounted to the weapon. Useful in environments where darkness is the enemy's advantage. The obvious tradeoff: the light that helps you see also shows everyone where you are. Running a flashlight in a dark environment is a choice about priorities.

**Biometrics** — A grip sensor and firing mechanism lock that reads the registered user's biometric profile on contact. Anyone else who picks up the weapon and tries to fire it gets nothing. Particularly useful for operators who worry about their weapons being turned against them — or for employers who want to ensure their operators' weapons stay their operators' weapons.

**Angel Mod** — Hammerlock's plasma-coated projectile system, installed by specialists who understand what they're working with and charge accordingly. The modification reinforces the weapon's barrel and action to handle the heat load of plasma-coated rounds, installs a powered magazine feed, and requires Angel Rounds exclusively — standard ammunition cannot be used in a modified weapon and attempting to do so jams it immediately.

### Ammunition

Standard ammunition is readily available from many fine stores throughout NYTE City. Bolts, magazines, grenades, and every other form of mischief you can find. Some ammunition is slightly more specialized, reflected in the availability or price point. Some can only be sourced from specialty dealers, and others have to be custom made and may cost you more than skrip.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| **Ammunition** | **Weapon Type** | **Tags** | **Availability** | **Cost** | **Notes** |
| Handgun Rounds | Handgun | — | Common | 15Ç/mag | — |
| SMG Rounds | SMG | — | Common | 20Ç/mag | — |
| Rifle Rounds | Rifle | — | Common | 20Ç/mag | — |
| Shotgun shells | Rifle (shotgun) | Spread | Common | 15Ç/box (10 shells) | Shot or slug — your call. It hurts either way. |
| Heavy Rounds | Heavy | — | Common | 50Ç/mag | Belt-fed weapons carry substantial loads. Treat as unlimited for standard encounters, resupply between operations. |
| Power Cell | Beam, Archery (Strix) | — | Uncommon | 50Ç/cell | Not interchangeable with ballistic ammunition. |
| Silver Rounds | Handgun, Rifle, Heavy | Withering (Lycanthropes) | By Practice | 3x standard | Standard ballistic damage against unaugmented targets. Withering against lycanthropes and kindred. |
| Holy Points | Handgun | Withering (Unholy) | By Practice | 4x standard | Hollow point notched with an isometric cross, blessed by faithful clergy. Withering damage against supernaturals aligned against the faith. |
| Angel Rounds | Handgun, Rifle, SMG | +4 DMG, AP, Burning, Agonized | Rare | 5x standard | Required for the Angel Mod. Plasma-coated high-grade alloy projectile. Cannot be used without the Angel Mod installed. |

**Handgun Rounds** — Standard ballistic ammunition for pistols and sidearms, available at every licensed vendor, corner kiosk, and grey-market dealer in NYTE City. If you carry a handgun, you carry these.

**SMG Rounds** — Higher-velocity pistol-caliber rounds optimized for the shorter barrels and higher cyclic rates of submachine guns. Common enough that running out is a planning failure, not a supply problem.

**Rifle Rounds** — Full-power rifle cartridges covering everything from battle rifles to sniper platforms. The round that most of NYTE City's serious work gets done with.

**Shotgun Shells** — Sold by the box and loaded by hand. Shot spreads, slugs punch — both options available at standard pricing, both equally unwelcome at close range.

**Heavy Rounds** — Belt-fed and bulk-purchased, heavy rounds are the ammunition of sustained operations rather than individual engagements. At 50Ç a load you're firing money at someone, which is why most operators save the heavy weapons for situations that justify the expense.

**Power Cell** — Rechargeable energy cells powering beam weapons and the Strix crossbow's firing mechanism. Not interchangeable with ballistic ammunition and not available at every corner store — plan your resupply before the job, not during it.

**Silver Rounds** — Standard ballistic performance against unaugmented targets; something considerably more permanent against lycanthropes and their kindred. The silver content doesn't make them hit harder — it makes the wounds stop healing. Only sold in specialty stores.

**Holy Points** — A hollow point notched with an isometric cross and blessed by clergy who know what they're blessing them for. Against supernaturals aligned against the faith, the damage doesn't regenerate — the blessing stays in the wound. Only sold in specialty stores.

**Angel Rounds** — Plasma-coated high-grade alloy projectiles that require the Angel Mod to fire and a specialist to source. When they work, nothing in their class hits harder or burns longer; when they don't, the weapon doesn't survive the conversation. Only sold in specialty stores.

## Melee Weapons

Close-quarters violence in NYTE City is fast, ugly, and rarely what anyone planned for. Melee weapons don't care about range, ammunition, or smart-targeting systems — they care about reach and the person swinging them. Whether that's a trained martial artist with a plasma katana or a runner with whatever came to hand, the math is the same: get close, hit hard, don't stop.

Two skills govern this section. Melee covers everything you can pick up, swing, or deploy without formal training in a specific tradition. Martial Arts covers weapons built around trained combat styles — tools that treat the fighter and the weapon as a single system. The weapons look different. The consequences don't.

All melee weapons — Melee and Martial Arts alike — add the wielder's BOD score to damage on a successful hit. A stronger character hits harder with a handheld weapon; a weaker one hits softer. The weapon sets the floor. The body behind it determines how far above that floor the damage lands.

### Melee

Knives, clubs, whips, and anything improvised that doesn't require formal training to swing. The Melee skill governs all of it, including the Parry action when you're on the receiving end. A higher Parry bonus means the weapon gives you something to work with defensively as well as offensively — a baton you can block with is a different tool than a whip you can't.

| Weapon | Skill | DMG | Style | Reach | Parry | Dam Type | Availability | Cost | Tags | Features |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Combat Knife | Melee | BOD+3 | Blade | 1m | — | Normal | Common | 100Ç | Conceal | — |
| Shock Knucks | Melee | BOD+4 | Blunt | 1m | — | Electric | Common | 350Ç | Stunning | — |
| Autobaton | Melee | BOD+6 | Blunt | 2m | +1 | Normal | Uncommon | 800Ç | Conceal | — |
| Razorwhip | Melee | BOD+6 | Blade | 1m | — | Normal | Rare | 1,600Ç | AP, Reach | — |
| Crusher | Melee | BOD+8 | Blunt | 1m | +1 | Electric | Rare | 2,800Ç | Stunning | — |
| Orion MW-1 "Filament" | Melee | BOD+10 | Blade | 2m | — | Energy | Exotic | 12,000Ç | AP, Reach | — |

**Combat Knife** — A fixed or folding blade in a belt sheath or jacket pocket. No frills, no tech, no modifications — just a sharp edge that fits in a space too small for anything more serious. The most common personal weapon in NYTE City and the last thing many people see coming.

**Shock Knucks** — A taser you can punch someone with. Brass knuckles threaded with a charge cell running through the striking surface. Simple, brutal, and easy to forget you're wearing until someone checks you for hardware.

**Autobaton** — An extendable security baton that collapses to jacket-pocket size and deploys in under a second. Standard issue for corporate corridor security and anyone who needs a weapon they can carry openly or conceal completely depending on the room.

**Razorwhip** — A length of monomolecular-edged cable on a reinforced grip, capable of parting light materials and leaving wounds that don't close cleanly. The people who carry these have usually learned not to touch the wire the hard way, and carry the scars to prove it.

**Crusher** — A heavily modified impact weapon built around an industrial vibration driver with an integrated electric discharge. Hits like a hydraulic press. Nobody picks up a Crusher because they want a fair fight.

**Orion MW-1 "Filament"** *(Monowire Whip — Orion Arms)* — A single filament of monomolecular wire on a powered reel, nearly invisible in motion and capable of parting light vehicle plating. Classified as a prohibited weapon in fourteen of NYTE City's twenty-two administrative zones. Orion describes it as "a precision cutting tool with tactical applications." Everyone who has seen it used describes it differently.

### Martial Arts

Weapons built around trained combat traditions — styles that treat the weapon as an extension of the fighter rather than a tool picked up in a hurry. The Martial Arts skill governs all of them, and the difference between a trained and untrained operator with these weapons is more pronounced than in almost any other category. A kusarigama in unpracticed hands is a liability. In the right hands, it is a system.

| Weapon | Skill | DMG | Style | Reach | Parry | Dam Type | Availability | Cost | Tags | Features |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Carbon Fiber Bo Staff | Martial Arts | BOD+4 | Blunt | 2m | +1 | Normal | Common | 250Ç | Knockdown, Reach | 2H |
| Kusarigama | Martial Arts | BOD+5 | Blade/Blunt | 2m | +1 | Normal | Uncommon | 900Ç | Disarming, Reach | 2H |

**Carbon Fiber Bo Staff** — Lightweight, durable, and unassuming until it isn't. A common training weapon that transitions cleanly into real application — the reach at 2m is more significant than most opponents account for until they're already on the floor.

**Kusarigama** — A weighted chain attached to a short-bladed weapon, the design unchanged for centuries because the design works. The chain creates disarming opportunities most opponents don't anticipate until the weapon they were holding is on the ground; the blade closes the distance after.

**Tekko-Kagi** — A strapped hand fitting of hardened composite, extending into raking blades along the dorsal hand and fingers. Compact enough to pass visual inspection in low-scrutiny environments when the hands are relaxed. The name is centuries old. The materials are not.

**Vibro Sai** — A traditional three-pronged weapon with a micro-vibration generator in the central blade. Built to trap, deflect, and penetrate in equal measure — opponents who try to block a Vibro Sai tend to regret the attempt.

**Shock Eskrima Sticks** — Paired hardwood-composite striking sticks with integrated charge cells along the striking surface. Standard Eskrima training translates directly; the shock is an upgrade layered onto a system that already works. Popular in underground fighting circuits for reasons that become obvious quickly.

**BDF Kōen** *(Plasma Katana — Bushido Defenceworks)* — *Kōen*: crimson flame. A traditionally-proportioned blade with a plasma-sheathed edge, built to be kept for a lifetime and used accordingly. Anyone carrying one has either earned it or taken it from someone who did, and either story is worth knowing.

## Ranged Weapons

Every ranged weapon entry includes an Accuracy (ACC) value — a bonus applied to aimed, single-shot attacks. Burst and full-auto fire trade that precision for volume; ACC does not apply in those modes.

Range bands — Close, Short, Medium, Long, Extreme — are defined in the Combat chapter. Firing beyond effective range imposes penalties to ACC. At sufficient distance, even a well-tuned weapon becomes wishful thinking.

### Handguns

Compact, concealable, and street-legal in most zones. The sidearm is the most common personal weapon in NYTE City — worn openly by licensed security, tucked into jacket lining by everyone else. At the low end, a handgun is whatever the city had available when you needed one. At the high end, it's a precision instrument that costs more than most people earn in two months. The difference isn't just damage. It's what you're willing to carry every day, and what you need it to do when the moment arrives.

| ADS LP-9 "Viper" | Handguns | 6 | +2 | Low | S/B | 15+1 | 2 | Common | 1,200Ç | — | Conceal |

**"Cheapshot"** *(Various)* — Not a gun so much as a category. Cheapshots are assembled from surplus components, unlicensed prints, and grey-market parts by a hundred different producers who share nothing except a price point. The city decided years ago that all of them were the same thing and named them accordingly. They come loaded. When they're empty, most people don't bother reloading.

**ADS LP-9 "Viper"** *(Light Pistol)* — Sleek, lightweight, and sized for a jacket pocket without printing. The Viper is the choice of corporate protection details and anyone who needs a weapon they can forget they're carrying until the moment they need it. Fast on the draw, accurate at close range, and built to Aegis's uncompromising fit-and-finish standards. Don't ask it to punch through body armor.

**VS-4 "Ironside"** *(Standard Pistol)* — Vanguard doesn't make elegant weapons; they make weapons that work. The Ironside is the sidearm that professionals pick up when they need something reliable for a long assignment and don't want to think about it again. It won't impress anyone at the range. It also won't jam in a drainage tunnel at 3 a.m. when the temperature is wrong and the magazine is dirty.

**AP-7 "Sentry"** *(Smart Pistol)* — Argus's AI-assisted targeting makes the Sentry the most accurate handgun on this list at any price point, compensating actively for movement, stress tremor, and environmental interference rather than just providing a good barrel. Three mod slots make it the most customizable handgun in its class. The price reflects all of that, and Argus knows it.

**HK-5 "Breach"** *(Heavy Pistol)* — Hammerlock's entry into the heavy sidearm market looks like something a more refined manufacturer would have rejected in prototyping. It is not pretty. The engineering is blunt, the finish is utilitarian, and the Breach hits harder than anything else at this price in this category. It exists because sometimes that's the only specification that matters.

**BDF Oni** *(Heavy Pistol)* — Bushido Defenceworks makes weapons to be kept. The Oni is engraved at the slide, balanced to its owner's grip, and chambered for armor-penetrating rounds as standard. It is the most expensive handgun on this list by a significant margin, and it earns that price in stopping power, craftsmanship, and the kind of quiet confidence that comes from carrying something built to last longer than you will.

### Submachine Guns (SMG)

Favored by close-quarters operatives, corridor security, and anyone who needs to put a lot of rounds downrange in a confined space without lugging a rifle. SMGs trade range and raw stopping power for volume, speed, and the kind of sustained fire that makes people stop moving. At the street end, a Chatter is a noise machine with a trigger. At the premium end, a Specter is a precision instrument that happens to fire thirty rounds on full-auto without losing control.

| "Chatter" | SMGs | 5 | +0 | Medium | S/B/F | 25+1 | 0 | Common | 300Ç | — | — |
| ADS CS-4 "Whisper" | SMGs | 5 | +2 | Medium | S/B | 30+1 | 2 | Uncommon | 2,200Ç | — | Suppressor |
| TS-7 "Bulldog" | SMGs | 6 | +1 | Medium | S/B/F | 30+1 | 1 | Common | 1,600Ç | — | — |
| HS-3 "Phantom" | SMGs | 7 | +1 | Medium | S/B/F | 25+1 | 1 | Uncommon | 3,200Ç | Volatile | — |

| ADS SR-1 "Specter" | SMGs | 6 | +2 | Medium | S/B/F | 30+1 | 2 | Rare | 6,000Ç | — | Suppressor |

**"Chatter"** *(Various)* — The SMG equivalent of a Cheapshot: assembled from whatever was available, named for what it does when you hold the trigger down. Nobody asks who made it. The answer is nobody in particular and everybody at once. Spray it in the right direction and hope the other person has somewhere to be.

**ADS CS-4 "Whisper"** *(Compact SMG)* — Built for covert operations and VIP protection details where noise is its own kind of problem. The Whisper runs single and burst only — full-auto would defeat the point — and its integrated suppressor brings the report down to something a neighboring room might not immediately identify. Accuracy at this damage level is the whole value proposition.

**TS-7 "Bulldog"** *(Tactical SMG)* — Vanguard's answer to every environment a rifle is too long for and a pistol isn't enough. The Bulldog is front-line hardware built for people who will use it every day in conditions that would ruin lesser weapons. It doesn't have the Whisper's quiet or the Phantom's punch, but it will be working long after both of those have given up.

**HS-3 "Phantom"** *(Hybrid SMG)* — Orion Arms describes the Phantom as "an experimental fusion of ballistic and directed-energy discharge." Operators in the field describe it as "the one that sometimes does something unexpected." Both descriptions are accurate. The damage output is real; so is the occasional misfire when the hybrid system decides the conditions aren't right. Operators who know what they're doing love it. Everyone else treats it carefully.

**VS-12 "Rampart"** *(Heavy SMG)* — Where the Bulldog is a rifle substitute, the Rampart is a squad support tool. The drum magazine keeps it running through sustained suppressive fire; the damage output at full-auto is enough to make people stay behind cover. It is not subtle, not concealable, and not designed for anyone who needs either of those things.

**ADS SR-1 "Specter"** *(Premium SMG)* — The Specter is what happens when Aegis applies the same engineering philosophy from their precision sidearms to a full-auto platform. Suppressed, accurate, and fully controllable on full-auto in a way that most weapons in this category are not. The price reflects the engineering hours, the tolerances, and the fact that Aegis knows exactly who buys this and what they use it for.

### Grenades

Thrown weapons for area denial, crowd control, and the moments when precision is less important than making a specific location temporarily uninhabitable. Grenades don't have accuracy ratings — throwing distance is always Short range, and where exactly they land is a function of the throw, the terrain, and occasionally the GM's sense of drama.

Manufactured grenades are reliable, consistent, and traceable. Junk Bombs are none of those things.

Grenade damage is fixed — the explosive charge determines the damage, not the thrower's physical strength. BOD Modifier does not apply to grenade damage. It may affect throwing range at the GM's discretion, but the blast radius and damage output are properties of the device, not the person deploying it.

**FG-1 "Thunderclap"** *(Hammerlock, Inc.)* — Hammerlock's standard fragmentation grenade: heavy, reliable, and built to end the conversation in a five-meter radius. The Thunderclap is the benchmark against which other frag grenades are measured, mostly because Hammerlock has been making them the same way for twenty years and sees no reason to change.

**SG-2 "Shockwave"** *(Aegis Defense Solutions)* — Non-lethal concussive grenade used for incapacitation, crowd control, and any situation where the objective requires the targets alive and cooperative afterward. The Shockwave's wide dispersal makes it effective in corridors and confined spaces; the same quality makes it inadvisable in rooms where your own team is present.

**EG-3 "Blackout"** *(Argus Defense Systems)* — Argus's electromagnetic pulse grenade, precision-engineered to disable electronics and cybernetic systems within its blast radius without the indiscriminate structural damage of a frag. The Blackout is the preferred tool of operators working against heavily augmented targets or hardened tech infrastructure. What it does to unshielded cyberware is not subtle.

**VS-3 "Curtain"** *(Vanguard Systems)* — A smoke grenade is the least exciting piece of kit on this list and among the most consistently useful. The Curtain generates a ten-meter obscurement cloud that lasts long enough to matter. Vanguard makes it in six colors. Most buyers choose grey.

**IG-7 "Cinder"** *(Hammerlock, Inc.)* — Incendiary grenade for area denial and the particular problem of targets who won't stop moving. The Cinder creates a sustained burn zone that applies ongoing damage each round until either the fire is extinguished or the target is no longer a concern. Hammerlock recommends against indoor use. This recommendation is frequently ignored.

|  |  |
|----|----|
| **Roll** | **Result** |
| 1 | **Frag** — It works. DMG 8, 5m radius. Jury-rigged but functional. |
| 2 | **Stun** — The flash fires, nothing else does. 10m radius, non-lethal. |
| 3 | **Smoke** — Not what you wanted. 10m obscurement cloud. Maybe useful. |
| 4 | **Dud** — Or it bounces back. GM's call. |

**"Junk Bomb"** *(Various)* — Somebody's best guess at a grenade, assembled from chemical components, scavenged casings, and optimism. The city sells them in unmarked bags from unmarked vendors, and nobody asks questions because at 75Ç nobody expects guarantees. When you throw a Junk Bomb, roll 1d4:

**Star Dust Grenade** — An adaptation developed by those who hunt lycanthropes and their kindred. The grenade disperses a cloud of silver-laced particulate that makes regeneration impossible for 1d4+1 minutes after inhalation, regardless of the target's supernatural recovery capabilities. Deals 1 damage per round while inside the cloud. Against non-lycanthrope targets the dust is a nuisance; against its intended targets, it is a cage.

**Sunburst Grenade** — A modified flashbang delivering a concentrated burst of UV radiation alongside the standard concussive discharge. The concussive effect applies to all targets in range; the UV burst applies Withering damage to undead who are susceptible to sunlight. The flash is real — everyone in range who lacks eye protection is affected by the concussive and visual disruption regardless of supernatural status.

### Rifles

Range is the rifle's argument. Where a handgun asks you to get close and an SMG asks you to get close fast, a rifle tells you to stay back and be patient — then makes the distance irrelevant. The Rifles skill covers three distinct weapon types that share that philosophy and not much else: urban combat rifles built for sustained firefights, shotguns built for the moment before the door comes off its hinges, and sniper rifles built for the shot nobody sees coming.

None of them are concealable. None of them are subtle. They reward the investment.

#### Urban Combat Rifles

The standard long arm of NYTE City — carried by corporate security on patrol, runners on high-stakes jobs, and anyone who expects to be outgunned by a handgun. Urban combat rifles balance damage and range against full-auto capability, giving operators the flexibility to engage at distance or pour rounds into a room when distance stops being an option.

|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| **Weapon** | **Skill** | **DMG** | **ACC** | **Range** | **RoF** | **Capacity** | **Mods** | **Availability** | **Cost** | **Tags** | **Features** |
| VR-8 "Sentinel" | Rifles | 7 | +1 | Long | S/B/F | 30+1 | 1 | Common | 2,800Ç | — | — |
| AR-9X "Guardian" | Rifles | 7 | +2 | Long | S/B/F | 30+1 | 1 | Uncommon | 4,500Ç | — | SMART Link |

**VR-8 "Sentinel"** *(Battle Rifle — Vanguard Systems)* — Vanguard's current production battle rifle: same philosophy as everything they make, updated tolerances, full-auto capability for operators who need it. The Sentinel is what front-line professionals carry when they expect to be in the field for a long time under conditions that would destroy more delicate hardware. It won't impress anyone at the range. It will still be working when more impressive hardware has given up.

**AR-9X "Guardian"** *(Assault Rifle — Argus Defense Systems)* — Argus's SMART Link integration earns its price here: the Guardian's AI targeting compensation translates a moving operator firing on a moving target into something that still groups acceptably at long range. Favored by elite government strike teams who want marksman precision without giving up full-auto capability. The SMART Link requires a compatible neural interface to fully utilize.

#### Shotguns

The shotgun's effective range is short and its argument is simple: at the distances where it operates, very little survives it. Where urban combat rifles are built for flexibility and sniper rifles are built for distance, shotguns are built for the specific geometry of a doorway, a corridor, or a room that needs to be cleared quickly and completely. The Spread tag means a well-placed shot can cover multiple targets — the tradeoff is that precision goes out the same window as everything else.

|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| **Weapon** | **Skill** | **DMG** | **ACC** | **Range** | **RoF** | **Capacity** | **Mods** | **Availability** | **Cost** | **Tags** | **Features** |
| "The Preacher" | Rifles | 8 | +0 | Low | S | 2 | 0 | Common | 400Ç | Spread | Conceal |
| SG-88 "Siege Breaker" | Rifles | 9 | +1 | Medium | S/B | 8+1 | 2 | Uncommon | 3,200Ç | Spread | — |

**"The Preacher"** *(Sawed-Off Shotgun — Various)* — A bible in one hand and a sawed-off in the other. The Preacher is not a specific model — it's what happens when someone takes a shotgun and removes everything that makes it inconvenient to carry, accepting the tradeoffs because the tradeoffs don't matter at the range where it gets used. Two rounds. No mod slots. No ACC bonus, because at that distance ACC is a formality. The city recognizes what it means when someone carries one openly and tends to find somewhere else to be.

**SG-88 "Siege Breaker"** *(Tactical Shotgun — Hammerlock, Inc.)* — Brutal and uncompromising, the Siege Breaker is Hammerlock's answer to close-quarters professional work. Semi-automatic with burst capability, eight rounds in the tube, and two mod slots for operators who want to build toward something specific. It is significantly heavier than a Preacher and significantly more capable. The name is accurate: at medium range with the right ammunition, it will breach most doors and the people standing behind them.

#### Sniper Rifles

Patience is the sniper rifle's first requirement. Everything else — the optics, the chambering, the hand-fitted tolerances of a BDF Ryū, the raw destructive reach of a Vanguard Verdict — is secondary to the discipline of waiting for the right moment and making the shot count. Sniper and anti-materiel rifles are single-fire only, low-capacity, and built around one premise: that distance is a weapon if you know how to use it.

**BDF Tora** *(Marksman Rifle — Bushido Defenceworks)* — A precision instrument built around a tradition of marksmanship that predates most of the technology surrounding it. BDF's engineering brings that tradition forward without losing it: advanced optics, a hand-fitted bolt mechanism, and a stock balanced to its owner's measurements if purchased direct. Single shot only, by design. The Tora is not a weapon for people in a hurry, and it does not pretend otherwise.

**BDF Ryū** *(Sniper Rifle — Bushido Defenceworks)* — The Ryū exists at a distance most weapons can't reach and most operators can't fully use. BDF builds it to specification, and modifying it would require understanding it first. Exotic availability is not a bureaucratic obstacle. It is a relationship.

<span class="mark">**VR-50 "Verdict"** *(Anti-Materiel Rifle — Vanguard Systems)* — The Verdict is not a sniper rifle. It shares the sniper rifle's patience and range, but where the Ryū and the Tora are built to kill people at distance, the Verdict is built to destroy things — light vehicles, reinforced cover, low-altitude aircraft, hardened entry points. The damage number reflects that: at extreme range, the Verdict delivers enough force to make most cover assessments irrelevant and most vehicle armor a polite suggestion. Vanguard built it for operators who need to reach out and end an argument about whether something was sturdy enough. It wasn't. The Verdict says so from a kilometer away.</span>

### Heavy Weapons

Heavy weapons exist outside the normal calculus of personal armament. They are not sidearms, not tactical tools, not options you weigh against other options. They are the point at which a firefight stops being a firefight and becomes a different kind of problem entirely — the kind measured in structural damage, evacuation radii, and how long it takes emergency services to stop asking questions and start filling out reports.

Hammerlock, Inc. builds most of what's on this list. That tells you everything about what this category is for. Vanguard provides the sustained-fire end — disciplined, military-grade suppression tools for operators who need to hold a position rather than level it. Everything else is Hammerlock. You call them when you're done being subtle.

All heavy weapons are Two-Handed. Most require a mount, bipod, or vehicle hardpoint for effective use.

| VHW-12 "Ironwall" | Heavy Weapons | 9 | +0 | Long | S/B/F | 200 (belt) | 1 | Rare | 9,500Ç | Suppression | Vehicle Mount |

**VLW-6 "Titan"** *(Light Support Weapon — Vanguard Systems)* — Belt-fed, bipod-equipped, and built for sustained suppressive fire across long engagements. The Titan is a squad support tool, not a solo weapon — its value is in the Suppression tag, keeping heads down while the rest of the team moves. Vanguard designed it for operators who need it to keep working after everything else has stopped, and it does. A hundred rounds before the belt runs dry, and Vanguard will sell you as many belts as you can carry.

**VHW-12 "Ironwall"** *(Heavy Machine Gun — Vanguard Systems)* — The step up from the Titan in every meaningful measurement: larger caliber, higher damage, greater sustained output, and a 200-round belt that turns a position into a problem. The Ironwall requires a proper mount — a bipod is not sufficient — which means it is a weapon for prepared positions, vehicle hardpoints, and operators who knew in advance that this was going to happen. When it opens up, the conversation about cover becomes academic.

**HGL-4 "Anvil"** *(Grenade Launcher — Hammerlock, Inc.)* — A six-round revolving grenade launcher that Hammerlock named after the thing that wins when the hammer hits it. The Anvil is an area denial and indirect fire tool: you aim it at the vicinity of the problem and let the blast radius handle the specifics. Accurate enough for an aimed shot at medium range; the 5m blast radius forgives the difference. Hammerlock makes the ammunition in four varieties. All of them are unpleasant.

**HRL-1 "Thunderhead"** *(Rocket Launcher — Hammerlock, Inc.)* — Single shot, shoulder-fired, and built for the specific problem of targets that are behind things they believe will protect them. The Thunderhead's 10m blast radius disagrees with most cover assessments, and its damage output at that radius makes the disagreement final. One round, then a full action to reload. Hammerlock's position is that if you needed more than one, you should have brought the Absolute.

**HFT-3 "Hellmouth"** *(Flamethrower — Hammerlock, Inc.)* — Ten bursts of sustained burning discharge in a forward cone, applicable to anything in the immediate area that Hammerlock's engineers have determined can be improved by being on fire. The Hellmouth does not do burst damage — it does ongoing damage every round until the target is no longer burning or no longer relevant. Hammerlock does not recommend indoor use. Field reports suggest this recommendation is not widely followed.

**HXC-1 "Absolute"** *(Siege Cannon — Hammerlock, Inc.)* — There is no diplomatic way to describe what the Absolute does. It is a man-portable siege weapon in the loosest interpretation of "portable," firing a single high-explosive round that produces a 15m blast radius and a damage output that makes the word "cover" stop meaning anything in the vicinity. Exotic availability is not a formality — Hammerlock sells the Absolute to specific clients for specific purposes, and the paperwork is extensive. When one appears in a scene, it is not a weapon. It is a weather event.

### Beam & Energy Weapons

Every weapon on this list runs on a power cell rather than ammunition, fires a directed energy discharge rather than a projectile, and does damage the ballistic weapons can't replicate exactly. That's the argument for beam weapons — not just different damage, but different effects. A laser doesn't knock someone back. A plasma round sets them on fire. A particle beam leaves nothing to identify. An EMP rifle doesn't care how tough you are; it cares how much of you is machine.

All beam weapons deal Energy damage. Energy damage interacts with armor differently than Normal or Electric damage — see the Damage Types callout for the full breakdown. Power cells are not interchangeable with ballistic ammunition and cannot be scavenged from a downed opponent's magazine pouch. Plan accordingly.

The Beam Weapons skill governs every entry in this section regardless of form factor.

#### Beam Sidearms

Five shots per cell, because each one draws the cell nearly dry. Orion describes it as "currently in extended field evaluation." That has been true for four years.

### Archery

The bow and the crossbow survive into 2099 for the same reason they survived every century before it: they are silent, they leave no ballistic signature, and they carry a payload that a bullet cannot. In a city blanketed with acoustic threat detection, electromagnetic surveillance, and security systems tuned to identify the discharge profile of every firearm on the market, an arrow is invisible in ways that matter. It doesn't announce itself. It just arrives.

That's the practical argument. The ritual argument is older and harder to quantify — certain targets require certain things, and for those targets the arrow is not a delivery system for kinetic force. It is a delivery system for something the target cannot regenerate, cannot shrug off, and cannot outlast. The right arrowhead against the right supernatural entity is not just damage. It is the specific shape of harm that thing has always been vulnerable to, arriving quietly from a distance.

The Archery skill governs all three platforms in this section. Arrows and bolts are purchased separately — see the Arrowheads & Bolts table below.

No manufacturer dominates this market because the design is simple enough that a dozen fabricators produce serviceable versions — what varies is the draw weight, the limb quality, and how well it holds zero on a rooftop at 3 a.m. in the rain. Operators who carry one have thought carefully about what a bow can do that a suppressed firearm can't, and have decided the answer justifies the weight of the quiver.

**BDF Yumi** *(Hybrid Longbow — Bushido Defenceworks)* — The Yumi is a traditional Japanese longbow reinterpreted in carbon fiber and smart-material composite limbs, hand-fitted to its owner's draw length and grip. BDF makes it the way they make everything: as if it will be kept, used, and eventually passed on. The longer range and higher damage reflect the platform's precision engineering rather than brute force — the Yumi rewards technique, and BDF builds it for operators who have the technique to reward. It is the only bow on this list that a BDF armourer will personally tune before delivery.

**ADS TC-1 "Strix"** *(Tactical Crossbow — Aegis Defense Solutions)* — Aegis named it after the owl, which hunts in silence and sees clearly in the dark. The Strix is a magazine-fed tactical crossbow with a folding stock for concealment, a scope rail, and a repeating bolt mechanism that allows burst fire without the draw cycle of a traditional bow. It is the most immediately accessible archery platform on this list — point, acquire, fire — and the most corporate in its execution. Clean lines, consistent performance, no tradition attached. Aegis builds tools, and the Strix is an exceptionally good one.

**Barbed Tip** — A hooked arrowhead designed to catch and tear on impact. The wound doesn't close cleanly. Causes Bleeding on a successful hit.

**Poison Tip** — A hollow-tipped arrowhead with a sealed payload chamber. Specify the payload at purchase — Poison, Sedative, or Paralytic. The tip delivers the payload on penetration; the condition applied depends on what's inside it.

**Withering** — Damage dealt by a Withering arrowhead cannot be regenerated by supernatural means. A werewolf struck by a silver-tipped arrow heals that wound the slow way, the human way, regardless of what their physiology would otherwise allow. The damage itself is not necessarily greater. The permanence is. *(Full Withering rules in the Combat chapter.)*

**By Practice** — Silver-Tipped, Iron-Cored, Consecrated, and Void-Touched arrowheads are not available through standard vendors. They are sourced through specialty shops that serve operators who know what they're hunting, or — in the case of Void-Touched — through practitioners with the specific knowledge and materials to prepare them. Most By Practice ammunition can be found if you know where to look; Void-Touched requires knowing the right person.

**Void-Touched** — The only arrowhead effective against the full range of supernatural targets, at the cost of reduced physical impact. The preparation process is not widely understood and the materials required are not widely available. Characters who carry Void-Touched ammunition have already had a conversation about what they're hunting that most people never need to have.

# Armor

Armor is the negotiation between what you can afford, what you can carry, and what you expect to be hit with. In NYTE City, that negotiation happens every time you get dressed — because the city doesn't care what you're wearing, but the things in it very much do.

Every piece of armor in this section is defined by four properties: what it's made of, how much of you it covers, how well it was made, and how hard it is to find. Those four factors determine everything else — how much punishment it absorbs, how long it lasts, and how much you can customize it.

### How Armor Works

**PROTECTION (PROT)** — Every time you take a hit, roll your armor's PROT die and subtract the result from incoming damage before it reaches you. PROT applies to all damage types. A 1d4 is a denim vest doing its best. A 1d8 is military-grade hardware doing exactly what it was built for.

**RESISTANCE (RES)** — A flat damage reduction that applies when your armor's type matches the incoming attack. All base armor is Kinetic — RES applies to Blade, Blunt, and Ballistic damage. RES does not apply to Energy or Magical damage unless the armor has been upgraded with Ablative or Warded treatments. *(See: Armor Upgrades)*

**INTEGRITY (INT)** — Armor is a resource. After any encounter where you took hits, roll a die determined by encounter difficulty and subtract the result from your armor's INT pool. When INT reaches zero, the armor is **Compromised** — PROT still rolls, but RES no longer applies until the armor is repaired.

- **Easy** — 1d4 loss

- **Medium** — 1d6 loss

- **Hard** — 1d8 loss

- **Legendary** — 1d10 loss

**Repairing Armor** — A Field Repair Kit restores 1d6 INT with roughly an hour of work. Full restoration requires a base or an armorer; time varies by quality. Some armor has special repair properties — see Mod Slots and Upgrades.

**Compromised** — Armor with 0 INT still rolls PROT but loses all RES until repaired. The armor is visibly damaged; the GM may apply social or environmental consequences accordingly.

### Armor Properties

**Quality** — Determines the PROT die, base INT pool, and base mod slots. Ranges from Low to High. Salvaged Armor is one category lower, Superior Armor is one category higher.

**Material** — Determines the RES bonus. Ranges from Light to Exotic.

**Coverage** — Determines what parts of the body the armor protects. Attacks targeting uncovered areas bypass armor entirely. Ranges from Light to Full.

**Rarity** — Determines availability and adds mod slots above the Quality baseline. Ranges from Common to Rare.

## Body Armor

### Light Coverage (Torso)

The baseline. A vest stops what it can reach — which is everything aimed at center mass and nothing aimed anywhere else. Light coverage is the most common armor in NYTE City because it's the easiest to wear under other clothing, the easiest to conceal, and the easiest to replace when it stops working.

**Reinforced Denim Vest** — Denim with a layer of ballistic padding stitched between the lining and the outer shell. It looks like a work vest because it mostly is one. Half the laborers in the industrial districts wear something similar without knowing it; the other half bought theirs specifically for the protection.

**Heavy Denim Vest** — A double-layered denim construction with a dense impact-absorbing core. Heavier than it looks, warmer than you want it to be in summer, and common enough that wearing one draws no attention whatsoever. The armor of people who can't afford to look like they're wearing armor.

**Kevlar Vest** — The entry point for purpose-built protection: a soft kevlar panel vest that stops most handgun rounds at close range and takes the edge off everything else. Standard issue for security contractors who don't rate hard plate. Gets the job done without pretending to do more.

**Urban Tactics Vest** — A modular soft armor vest with a MOLLE-compatible exterior and two upgrade slots for operators who want to build toward something specific. The vest itself is unremarkable; what you put on it isn't.

**Kevlar Reinforced Leather Vest** — Leather over a kevlar substrate, the construction giving it both the impact resistance of the synthetic and the cut resistance of the leather. More protection than either material alone, worn by people who need both and don't mind the weight.

**HD CF 200 Tactical Vest** — Carbon fiber plating over a kevlar backing in a low-profile carrier, the HD CF 200 is the vest that corporate security teams step up to when soft armor stops feeling sufficient. Three mod slots make it the most customizable standard vest on this list. Hammerlock makes the plates; someone else assembles the carrier.

**DarkSun Elite Undershirt** — A compression undershirt woven from DarkSun's proprietary impact-dispersing fiber, worn beneath street clothes without printing or adding visible bulk. High quality protection that looks like nothing at all. The choice of people who need to walk into rooms where wearing visible armor would end the conversation before it started.

**SpecOps Vest** — Military-grade hard plate carrier with front, back, and side protection in a heavy composite construction. Not subtle, not light, and not designed to be either. The vest that professionals reach for when the job has stopped being ambiguous about what it requires.

### Medium Coverage \*(Torso, Arms)\*

A jacket covers more ground and catches more of what a vest misses — arms are a common target in close quarters, and anything that makes a called shot to the shoulder less catastrophic is worth the extra weight. Medium coverage is the working professional's standard: enough protection to matter, enough freedom to move.

**Denim Jacket** — A denim jacket is a denim jacket. It stops a little of what it's going to stop and none of what it isn't. The city is full of people wearing one, which is its own kind of advantage — nobody looks twice, nobody clocks you as armored, and when it fails you can replace it for 125Ç.

**Leather Jacket** — Real leather over a synthetic impact layer, the kind of jacket that gets better with wear and provides marginally better protection than it has any right to. One mod slot for the operator who wants to add something without committing to a purpose-built rig. The most common piece of armor in NYTE City that doesn't look like armor at all.

**Road Warrior's Jacket** — Heavy reinforced leather with impact padding at the shoulders, elbows, and spine — originally designed for motorcycle riders, repurposed by everyone who spends time in places where being thrown against a wall is a professional hazard. The reinforcement is visible if you know what to look for. Most people don't.

**DarkSun Streetweave** — A mid-weight jacket woven from DarkSun's concealment fiber, the Streetweave sits at the intersection of street fashion and serious protection. It looks expensive because it is. It looks like armor to nobody, which is the entire point. Three mod slots give the operator room to build without compromising the silhouette.

**Ranger Protection Armor** — A heavy-duty protection jacket built for operators who spend time in environments that don't care about their comfort — field work, perimeter duty, extended outdoor operations. The weight is real and the protection justifies it. Not a city jacket; a working jacket that happens to work in the city.

**DarkSun JB-6 Sleekwear** — DarkSun's premium mid-tier concealment jacket: heavy protective fiber in a cut that reads as fashion rather than tactical. Worn beneath a blazer or over a shirt, the JB-6 disappears into whatever environment it's brought into. The people who wear it are precisely the people nobody would expect to be wearing armor.

**Plasteel Weave Jacket** — A high-quality tactical jacket with plasteel fiber woven through a medium-density carrier, the Plasteel Weave sits at the top of what you can wear into a business meeting and still feel protected leaving it. Purpose-built for operators who move between professional environments and dangerous ones, sometimes on the same evening.

**DarkSun Nightshade Armor** — DarkSun's flagship medium-coverage piece: high quality protection in a jacket that passes every visual inspection and most electronic ones. Pre-installed Concealable and Dampening features make it the choice of operators who need to be undetectable before, during, and after the job. Four mod slots. The Nightshade is not cheap, and the people who can afford it know exactly why they're paying for it.

### Full Coverage \*(Torso, Arms, Legs)\*

Full coverage armor is a statement as much as a choice — you're wearing it because you expect to be shot at, and you've accepted the weight and visibility that comes with that expectation. Dusters, combat suits, and full tactical rigs. The Ganglord's Trench tells the street something before you open your mouth. The Hammerlock Reaper Overcoat tells it something else entirely.

**Motorcycle Leathers** — A full riding suit in impact-padded leather covering torso, arms, and legs, worn by riders and repurposed by anyone who appreciates that motorcycle gear was designed around the assumption that the wearer would eventually hit something at speed. Practical, durable, and reads as exactly what it is — which in most neighborhoods is not a problem.

**Ganglord's Trench** — A long reinforced heavy coat with impact padding worked into the lining from collar to knee. The silhouette is distinctive and the protection is real. Nobody who sees someone wearing a Ganglord's Trench mistakes them for a civilian. That's often the point.

**Recon Unit Set** — A full light-armor set — jacket, pants, integrated coverage — designed for operators who need to move quickly across difficult terrain while maintaining protection. The light material keeps the weight down; the full coverage keeps the exposed surface area low. Built for people who expect to be outside the wire for extended periods.

**Security Rig** — The standard full-coverage armor set of corporate security contractors and private protection firms: recognizable, professional-looking, and protective enough for the environments most security work actually involves. Common enough that wearing one reads as employed rather than threatening.

**Reinforced Merc Duster** — A long reinforced coat with medium-density protective panels from shoulders to shins, the Merc Duster is the armor of choice for operators who want full coverage without looking like they're wearing a tactical rig. The duster silhouette is city-common enough to blend; the reinforcement underneath is not.

**Guardian Suit** — A heavy full-coverage protection suit built for sustained use in hostile environments — the kind of armor you wear when the job description includes "sustained contact with armed opposition." Uncomfortable for extended wear, indifferent to that fact, and protective enough to justify both.

**BDF Viper Stealth Suit** — A full-coverage suit in BDF's lightweight concealment fiber, the Viper is what the Ronin wears when the job requires moving through the city undetected and fighting when detected. Pre-installed Concealable and Dampening features make it invisible to most detection systems. Four mod slots and BDF craftsmanship make it the platform for operators who build their kit around a specific philosophy rather than a general purpose.

**HD Recon Stealth Armor** — Full-coverage medium armor optimized for extended reconnaissance operations: sensor-dampened, communication-integrated, and built to keep an operator in the field and in contact with their team for hours without compromising their position. The HD Recon is the armor of professionals who gather information for a living and understand that being found defeats the purpose.

**Hammerlock Reaper Overcoat** — A full-length heavy armor overcoat that looks like it was built to survive whatever it's going to be put through, because it was. Pre-installed Self-Healing and Magnetic Stow Point mean the Reaper arrives ready to work and stays that way. Hammerlock builds it for operators who expect heavy contact and intend to walk away from it. At 4,000Ç it is the most expensive off-the-shelf armor on this list, and it earns the price every time someone puts it on and doesn't take it off until the job is done.

## Head & Hand Equipment

Head and hand protection operate differently from body armor — they don't roll PROT or track INT. Instead, each piece provides a specific defensive feature, immunity, or enhancement. A helmet doesn't absorb damage the way a vest does; it changes the *nature* of damage taken to the head, or provides capabilities that change what the wearer can do.

**Motorcycle Helmet** — A full-face motorcycle helmet offers more head protection than most people in NYTE City bother with, costs less than a decent meal out, and raises no eyebrows in any neighborhood that has regular vehicle traffic. The visor scratches easily. Replace it when it does.

**Ballistic Nylon Helmet** — A purpose-built ballistic helmet in nylon composite, the kind worn by security contractors and private military personnel who have decided that head protection is worth the visibility cost. Common enough in professional contexts that it reads as employed. Effective enough to justify wearing.

**M-88A2 Enhanced Helmet** — A heavy ballistic helmet with an integrated chinstrap retention system and mount points for accessories. Military surplus in origin, still military-grade in performance. The kind of helmet that survives the jobs it was worn for and gets passed to the next operator when the previous one no longer needs it.

**Sentinel Vanguard Helmet** — A sealed tactical helmet with filtered environmental systems providing complete immunity to gas, sonic disruption, and dazzle weapons. The seal is the feature — once it's on and locked, what's outside stays outside. Vanguard builds it for operators who expect the environment itself to be weaponized against them.

**Ghostsuit Helmet** — A high-end sensor-integrated helmet with configurable IR, UV, and thermal imaging capability built into the visor. The world looks different through a Ghostsuit — sometimes literally. Augmentable for additional sensor packages with the right slot investment. The choice of operators who treat information as primary and visibility as a secondary concern.

**Hacking Visor** — A custom-fabricated interface visor that integrates directly with electronic systems, providing enhanced interaction capabilities and a significant skill bonus when interfacing with electronic locks, terminals, and networks. Not available through standard channels. The people who use these know how to find them.
