| SMARTLink Gloves | High | Exotic | Rare | 2,800Ç | +2 ACC when using SMARTLink-compatible weapons |
| PrecisionGrip Gloves | High | Exotic | Rare | 2,500Ç | +2 to precision skill checks |

**InfernoShield Gloves** — Heavy composite gloves rated for brief contact with high-temperature surfaces and sustained exposure to heat sources. Designed for industrial environments and repurposed everywhere fire is a professional concern. The rating is honest: six seconds of immunity is longer than it sounds when something is actively burning you.

**ZapGrip Gloves** — Faraday-woven heavy gloves providing complete electrical isolation for brief contact with live systems and significant damage reduction for sustained exposure. The choice of operators who work with powered systems under hostile conditions — or who expect to be hit by weapons that deliver their damage through contact discharge.

**ChemGuard Gloves** — Acid-resistant composite gloves rated for brief immersion in corrosive substances and significant protection against sustained chemical exposure. Standard in laboratory and industrial environments; useful in any situation where the opposition has decided that chemistry is an appropriate weapon.

**Hacking Gloves** — Exotic interface gloves with embedded sensor arrays and haptic feedback systems that enhance the operator's ability to interact with electronic systems at the physical level. Useful for lockwork, terminal access, and any situation where the difference between success and failure is how well you can feel what you're doing.

**SMARTLink Gloves** — Interface gloves that extend a weapon's SMARTLink AI targeting system through the grip, providing active compensation and enhanced accuracy on any SMARTLink-compatible weapon. The gloves don't aim for you — they make sure that when you aim, the connection between your intent and the weapon's output is as clean as engineering can make it.

**PrecisionGrip Gloves** — High-sensitivity haptic gloves that enhance fine motor feedback for any precision task — surgery, lockpicking, electronics work, or any situation where the margin between success and failure is measured in millimeters. Worn by professionals who treat their hands as instruments and are willing to pay for the upgrade.

### Armor Features & Upgrades

Armor can be enhanced beyond its base stats through two mechanisms: **Features** that come pre-installed by the manufacturer, and **Upgrades** installed by an armorer after purchase. Features are part of the armor's construction — they don't occupy mod slots and cannot be removed. Upgrades consume mod slots. Low quality armor has no mod slots and cannot be upgraded. Mid quality armor has slots available but no pre-installed features. High quality armor arrives with manufacturer features already built in, with all mod slots remaining open for further customization.

All upgrades require installation by a licensed or black-market armorer. The exception is **Rapid Repair** — swapping modular plates is a field action, no armorer required.

#### Features

Pre-installed by the manufacturer on select armor. Part of the purchase price. Do not occupy mod slots.

**Concealable** — The armor is thin and lightweight enough to be worn discreetly beneath a hoodie, blazer, or similar outer layer without printing or triggering visual identification as armor. Standard security visual checks do not detect it; specialized scanning equipment or a successful Perception check against a defined threshold may. DarkSun's primary engineering focus.

**Dampening (Thermal / Optical / Sound)** — Specifically engineered to reduce detection by sensors. The armor's surface disperses heat signatures, reduces optical reflection, and dampens sound transmission. Grants +1 to Stealth checks against sensor-based detection. Specify type at manufacture — a single Dampening feature covers one detection type.

**Integrated Comms** — A communications system built into the armor using a throat mic and earpiece, allowing hands-free coordination with partners without requiring a separate device. Encrypted by default at the armor's quality tier.

**Magnetic Stow Point** — One or more high-strength magnetic mounting points on the armor's surface for hands-free storage of metallic objects — a rifle across the back, a vibrobat at the hip, a sidearm at the chest. Items stored this way can be drawn as a free action in combat.

**Rapid Repair** — The armor is constructed with modular panels that can be swapped in the field when damaged. Using a Field Repair Kit on armor with Rapid Repair is an Action rather than requiring extended downtime. No armorer needed for field swaps.

**Self-Healing** — Advanced materials woven through the armor automatically regenerate INT over time. After each encounter, roll 1d4 — on a 3 or higher, the armor regains 1d4 INT without requiring a repair kit or armorer. Cannot restore INT beyond the armor's maximum.

**Headshot Defense** — When wearing a helmet with this feature, called shots to the head are treated as hits to the torso for damage purposes. The helmet absorbs the directional advantage of the shot; the body armor (if any) still applies normally.

**Gas / Sonic / Dazzle Immunity** — The sealed environment of the Sentinel Vanguard Helmet provides complete immunity to atmospheric effects, sonic disruption, and visual dazzle weapons. What gets in has to get through the seal first.

**Augmentable Senses** — The Ghostsuit Helmet's sensor suite can be configured for infrared, ultraviolet, or thermal imaging. Switching modes is a free action. All three can be active simultaneously with the right upgrade installed.

**Elemental Immunity** — InfernoShield, ZapGrip, and ChemGuard gloves provide full immunity to their respective damage type for exposures under six seconds — a quick contact, a brief grip, a short-duration burst. Sustained exposure beyond six seconds reduces to 50% damage reduction. These gloves are rated for the hands only; the rest of the body remains unprotected.

**SMARTLink Gloves** — These integrate directly with SMARTLink-compatible weapons, extending the AI targeting system through the grip interface. The +2 ACC stacks with weapon-native SMARTLink bonuses where both are present.

#### Upgrades

Installed by an armorer. Each upgrade costs one mod slot and a Çredits cost determined by the armorer and the upgrade type. Quality restrictions apply where noted.

**Ablative Plating** — A series of hexagonal panels fitted over the armor's surface with a subtle iridescent sheen. When struck by energy-based attacks, the plating absorbs and disperses the discharge. Grants the armor's full RES bonus against Energy damage in addition to its standard Kinetic application. Minimum quality: Mid.

**EMP Shielding** — Conductive wire woven through the armor's lining provides protection against electromagnetic pulse attacks. Grants +10% EMP resistance. Particularly relevant for characters with significant cyberware — shielded armor reduces cascade failure risk when hit by EMP sources.

**HUDsync** — When paired with a HUDsync-compatible helmet, a Heads-Up Display appears within the visor showing real-time armor status, weapon systems, and linked device information. Requires a compatible helmet; the upgrade in the armor provides the transmitter, not the display. The Ghostsuit Helmet is HUDsync compatible.

**Resistance (Thermal / Electric / Freezing)** — Specialized lining that provides significant protection against a specific environmental damage type. Grants 50% damage reduction against heat, electric, or cold-based attacks. Specify type at installation — each Resistance upgrade covers one damage type. Multiple Resistance upgrades can be installed in separate slots.

**Tri-Weave** — A nano-fiber triple-weave mesh worked into the armor's structure, dramatically increasing durability without meaningful weight addition. Grants +10 INT to the armor's integrity pool. Can be installed multiple times in separate slots for cumulative effect. Minimum quality: Mid.

**Warding** — Magical protection imbued into the armor by a practitioner with the knowledge and materials to do so. Extends the armor's RES bonus to magical damage. Cannot be purchased with Çredits alone — requires finding a practitioner willing to perform the work. By Practice. Minimum quality: Mid.

#### Pre-Installed Features by Armor

The following High quality and select Rare Mid quality armors come with manufacturer features pre-installed. Features do not occupy mod slots — all listed mod slots remain available for upgrades.

|----|----|----|
| **Armor** | **Pre-Installed Features** | **Mod Slots Available** |

| SpecOps Vest | Rapid Repair | 3 |
| DarkSun Streetweave | Concealable | 3 |
| DarkSun JB-6 Sleekwear | Concealable | 3 |
| Plasteel Weave Jacket | Tri-Weave | 3 |
| DarkSun Nightshade Armor | Concealable, Dampening | 4 |

# Equipment

Weapons and armor handle the violence. Equipment handles everything else — the tools that get you into the room, the medicine that keeps you functional after the room goes wrong, the transport that gets you out before anyone asks questions. In NYTE City, being well-equipped isn't optional. It's the difference between a professional and someone who used to be one.

This section covers the everyday and specialist equipment available to operators, civilians, and everyone in between. Prices reflect street or commercial value. Some items are available at any corner kiosk; others require knowing where to look.

## Tech & Communications

Personal technology and communications equipment. In 2099 the distinction between a communication device, a computer, and a field tool has largely collapsed — your commlink is your slate is your AR display. The items below cover the full spectrum from everyday civilian tech to specialist operator hardware.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| **Item** | **Availability** | **Cost** | **Notes** |
| Slate | Common | 250Ç | Handheld PC and commlink |
| Monocle | Common | 375Ç | Retractable AR lens |
| CommLINK | Common | 95Ç | Standard field radio link |
| MC-Radio | Common | 520Ç | Small radio transceiver |
| SMART Brace | Common | Varies | Wrist-mounted comms platform |
| Subvocal CommLINK | Uncommon | 385Ç | Short range encrypted, throat-mounted |
| SMART Link | Uncommon | 150Ç | Neural-device interface |
| SMART Deck I | Common | 800Ç | Entry LINK/terminal rig, +1 Interface |
| SMART Deck II | Uncommon | 2,200Ç | Professional LINK/terminal rig, +2 Interface |
| SMART Deck III | Rare | 5,500Ç | Specialist LINK/terminal rig, +3 Interface |
| Nanotech Disguise Kit | Rare | 2,800Ç | Single use, 1 hour, full body |
| Energy Shield Cartridge | Rare | 1,800Ç | Single use, SMART Brace required |

**Slate** — The standard mobile device of NYTE City: part handheld PC, part commlink, part everything else. Runs standard applications, connects to public networks, and does most of what a person needs to do digitally without requiring implants or specialist hardware. Common enough that not having one is the unusual choice.

**Monocle** — A retractable lens worn over one eye providing video conferencing, augmented reality overlays, and heads-up data display. Ubiquitous enough in professional environments that wearing one draws no attention. Most people forget they have it on until someone calls.

**CommLINK** — A standard radio link for field operations: straightforward, reliable, and unencrypted. Anyone with the right equipment can listen in. The choice of operators who need comms more than they need security, or who are running in environments where encryption isn't the concern.

**MC-Radio** — A small handheld radio transceiver for basic communication over moderate distances. More range than a CommLINK, less capability than a Cryp-Deck, and simple enough that anyone can operate it without training. The backup comms device that professionals carry and hope they never need to use.

**SMART Brace** — A wrist-mounted computer and communications platform running on SMART Link protocol. Makes calls, receives data, interfaces with compatible devices, and accepts cartridge attachments for expanded functionality — including the Energy Shield Cartridge. The platform most operators build their tech loadout around, not because it's the best device available, but because it works with everything else. Price varies by configuration and vendor.

**Subvocal CommLINK** — A throat-mounted encrypted radio link that picks up subvocalizations rather than audible voice. Short range, completely silent from the outside. The choice for operators who need to communicate in environments where being heard making a call would end the operation.

**SMART Link** — A neural interface that connects the user to SMART-compatible devices and weapons, enabling full SMART Targeting integration and high-tier tech interactions. The implant itself is a minor installation; what you connect it to is where the investment begins. *(Minor cybernetic procedure — see the Cybernetics chapter for full details.)*

**SMART Deck I** — The entry-level terminal intrusion rig. Runs basic programs sufficient for standard lock interfaces, low-security terminals, and unencrypted systems. The SMART Deck I is what most street-level operators carry when they expect to need terminal access and aren't planning on hitting anything hardened. Grants +1 to Interface checks when hacking terminals or operating in The LINK.

**SMART Deck II** — A professional-grade intrusion platform running more sophisticated programs and handling higher-security terminal environments. The choice of operators who work The LINK regularly and need something that won't fail them when the security is better than expected. Grants +2 to Interface checks when hacking terminals or operating in The LINK.

**SMART Deck III** — Specialist hardware for serious terminal intrusion. The tool of DeKODERs and Digilantes who operate at the serious end of The LINK — runs complex programs against hardened corporate and military-grade systems. Not a casual purchase and not carried by anyone who doesn't know exactly what they're doing with it. Grants +3 to Interface checks when hacking terminals or operating in The LINK.

**Nanotech Disguise Kit** — A single-use aerosol applicator containing nanoscale surface-alteration agents that restructure the appearance of skin, hair, and clothing across the full body. Visually convincing for approximately one hour before the nanites degrade. Does not alter biometrics — retinal scanners, palm readers, and DNA analysis see through it without difficulty. Useful against humans who use their eyes; useless at any checkpoint that doesn't.

**Energy Shield Cartridge** — A single-use cartridge that slots into a SMART Brace and auto-triggers against incoming ballistic or kinetic attacks. When struck, the cartridge deploys an energy field that fully absorbs the damage from one hit — but not the force behind it. The impact still arrives. Make a BOD Essence Check TN8 TH1 or be Knocked Down. The cartridge is consumed on activation regardless of the result. One hit, one use, no reloading mid-fight.

## Field & Recovery

The equipment that keeps operators functional — medically, mechanically, and mentally. Combat takes a toll on bodies, gear, and minds in equal measure, and this section covers the tools for addressing all three.

Most of what follows is a battle chem: something you put into yourself in about a second, that works immediately, and that charges for it later. NYTE City runs on them the way it runs on Çredits — quietly, constantly, and with the bill arriving later than anyone plans for. What separates a professional from a casualty is rarely whether they use them. It's whether they knew what it was going to cost before they pushed the plunger.

Nothing on this page requires a check. What each one costs you in action is in the table.

Sustained use leaves marks. Not a dose and not a bad night — months of it. None of it washes off, fades with a clean week, or answers to anything a street doc can do, and everyone in this city knows how to read it. A crew can tell what a stranger has been living on before he finishes crossing the room.

| **Item** | **Availability** | **Cost** | **Action** | **Notes** |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Silver Card | Common | 800Ç | Fast | Emergency medical beacon — 5 minute response |
| Nanomed Kit | Uncommon | 4,500Ç | Fast | Clears Conditions, stabilizes, regenerates for BOD rounds |
| Quickstitch | Common | 1,500Ç / strip of 5 | Fast | +2 Health Levels for the scene, 1 comes back out |
| Slowstitch | Common | 1,000Ç / strip of 5 | Fast | +1 Health Level per dose, an hour owed per dose |
| Speed Heal | Common | 2,100Ç / dose | Fast | 2× healing rate for 24 hours |
| Anodyne "Hush" | Common | 250Ç | Fast | −1 Pain Level for 1d4 rounds |
| Veloxin-12 "Red" | Rare | 900Ç | Fast | +3 REF Skill Checks, then −3 |
| Somatrex-8 "Green" | Uncommon | 600Ç | Fast | +3 BOD Skill Checks, then −3 |
| Cerebryx-5 "Blue" | Uncommon | 600Ç | Fast | +3 INT Skill Checks, then −3 |
| Aurexa-3 "Yellow" | Uncommon | 600Ç | Fast | +3 MAG Skill Checks, then −3 |
| Detoxifier "DT" | Uncommon | 400Ç | Fast | Flushes everything, causes Agonized |
| Mindscape Visor | Common | 650Ç | 1 hour | Doubles SAN recovery rate |
| Field Repair Kit | Common | 300Ç | 1 hour | Restores 1d6 armor INT |
| Cybernetics Maintenance Kit | Uncommon | 1,200Ç | Downtime | +5 Cybertech, reduces rejection |
| Weapons Maintenance Kit | Common | 200Ç | Downtime | +1 ACC after cleaning |

**Silver Card** — Healthcare that fits in your wallet. Snap the card and an emergency beacon goes up; EMTs are en route and at your location inside five minutes. The Silver Card doesn't treat anything itself, it summons people who will. Widely available, widely carried, and the first thing operators check for before a job that might go sideways.

- Summons EMTs to your location within 5 minutes, who provide Medical Check at 20, Nanomed Kits, and airlift you for Focused Healing

*See Downtime for additional information*

**Nanomed Kit** — A pressurized injector loaded with targeted nanites. Where Speed Heal tells the body to work faster, the Nanomed goes in and does the work itself: sealing vessels, flushing toxins, and quieting the nerve traffic that turns an injury into agony.

- Clears Bleeding, Poisoned, and Agonized, stabilizes a Dying character, and starts a regeneration of 1 HP per round for BOD rounds.

- Additional doses within twenty-four hours still clear Conditions and stabilize, but the regeneration thins out. A second kit inside a day regenerates 1 HP per two rounds, a third 1 HP per three, and so on.

**Quickstitch** — A pressurized shot of adrenaline and coagulant, sold in strips of five. It doesn't repair damage. It floods the system hard enough to keep a wounded operator upright and seals surface wounds enough to slow blood loss, and it stops working when the adrenaline does.

- Restores 2 Health Levels per dose for the remainder of the scene.

- Pain Level is unchanged, and remains set by the damage taken.

- At the end of the scene, 1 Health Level is lost per dose taken. If this empties the last Health Level, the character falls Unconscious rather than Dying.

- No effect on a character already at zero Health Levels. Does not clear Bleeding.

- **Sustained use:** wounds closed under a stitch close badly — heavy raised scarring in places nothing should have scarred at all.

**Slowstitch** — A regenerative compound sold in strips of five. Where Quickstitch borrows against the body, Slowstitch drives it, forcing tissue repair at a rate it can't sustain and collecting the difference in rest once the pressure is off.

- Restores 1 Health Level per dose. The healing is permanent.

- One dose per Action. A full strip takes five Actions, which inside an encounter means most of three rounds.

- After the scene, the user owes one hour of rest per dose taken. A user who stays active instead is Agonized until the rest is taken.

- **Sustained use:** Tissue made to knit that quickly sometimes knits wrong. Old injuries sit badly, joints don't track, and a body that's had enough of it moves like one twenty years older than the file says.

**Speed Heal** — Healthcare in a syringe. Speed Heal accelerates the body's natural healing to twice the normal rate for twenty-four hours. It does not clear any Conditions, so anyone Bleeding out will still need help, as Speed Heal’s benefit is measured in hours not seconds.

- Grants 2x Natural Healing rate for 24 hours, does not clear any Conditions.

- Can be used up to 3 consecutive days without consequences.

- **Sustained Use:** At day 4 of consecutive use, users can develop the Addiction Disadvantage. Must pass BOD Essence Check TN8 TH 2+1 TH per additional day. Failure results in Addiction Disadvantage at Rank 1, or +1 Rank if you already have it.

*See Downtime for additional information*

**Anodyne "Hush"** — A fast-acting nerve block. It suppresses pain signaling without touching the injury underneath, which remains exactly as severe as it was. Standard in field medical kits, where a crewmate who can think clearly is worth more than one who can feel accurately.

- Reduces Pain by one level for 1d4 rounds, including Pain contributed by Agonized. Pain cannot drop below 0.

- The GM rolls the duration and does not reveal it.

- **Sustained use:** the nerves come back wrong. It starts as a tremor in the hands that only shows when they're at rest, and then it stops waiting for rest. It doesn't fade when you stop taking it, and anybody whose work depends on steady hands can read it across a table.

**Hillcrest Boosters** — Red, Green, Blue, Yellow. Four performance compounds sold by prescription, each targeting a single attribute. Hillcrest markets them as treatments for legitimate deficiencies, and for a small number of patients that's what they are. On the street they're known by color, after what long-term use does to the people taking them.

- +3 to the listed Skill Checks for 1d4 rounds.

- When the effect lapses, −3 to the same Skill Checks for an equal number of rounds.

- The GM rolls the duration and does not reveal it. The user is told on the round it's about to lapse.

- **Sustained use:** Red eyes, green fingertips, blue lips, or the jaundice that comes with yellow. It shows faintly at first and then it doesn't. Every fixer, guard, and receptionist in NYTE City knows what those mean, and some doors get cheaper while most get considerably more expensive.

- **Chasing the rainbow:** There's a window as one booster fades where the next can be caught clean — the new rush arriving before the old one lets go, and no crash in between. The reality is the crashes are delayed and all come at once as soon as the final boost fades.

**Detoxifier "DT"** — A combined chelating agent and diuretic that strips foreign substances out of the bloodstream. Sold widely and without questions. Indiscriminate, unpleasant, and effective, in that order.

- Ends all chems, toxins, and nanites currently active in the user's system, including any substance suppressing another effect. Clears **Poisoned**.

- Inflicts **Agonized** for one hour.

- Beneficial effects end as well. Borrowed Health Levels from Quickstitch are lost immediately, booster crashes begin at once, Nanomed regeneration stops, and suppressed Pain returns.

- Does not remove the Addiction Disadvantage. Clearing the substance only begins withdrawal early.

- Does not remove sustained-use marks.

**Mindscape Visor "The Drift"** — A full-immersion VR meditation visor that plays therapeutic environments calibrated to accelerate psychological recovery. Operators who have seen too much too fast use it between jobs to stay functional.

- Doubles the rate of SAN recovery while in use.

- Requires minimum of 1 hour of use

*See Downtime for additional information*

**Field Repair Kit** — A compact tool kit for emergency armor maintenance in the field. 5 uses.

- Restores 1d6 INT to one piece of armor with roughly an hour of work.

- Armor with the Rapid Repair feature restores INT as an Action rather than requiring the full hour.

**Cybernetics Maintenance Kit** — A specialist toolkit for the upkeep and field repair of cybernetic implants. Regular maintenance reduces implant rejection rates and addresses minor component damage sustained in combat.

- Grants +5 to Cybertech skill checks when performing maintenance.

> *Full cybernetic maintenance rules in the Cybernetics chapter.*

**Weapons Maintenance Kit** — Cleaning tools, lubricants, and replacement components for keeping firearms and other weapons performing at specification. A well-maintained weapon is a reliable weapon; the kit represents the difference between a piece that groups tight and one that jams when you need it most.

- Grants +1 ACC on the next combat encounter after a full cleaning session.

## Tools & Field Gear

The equipment that gets you from point A to point B when point B doesn't want you there. Entry tools, movement gear, and the general-purpose hardware that operators reach for when the situation requires something other than a weapon.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| **Item** | **Availability** | **Cost** | **Notes** |
| Multitool | Common | 85Ç | General purpose field tool |
| Crowbar | Common | 45Ç | Mechanical entry, improvised weapon |
| Cutting Torch | Common | 320Ç | Heavy entry, cuts locks and hinges |
| Grappling Hook | Common | 180Ç | Vertical access, rooftop entry |
| Climbing Gear | Common | 450Ç | Extended vertical operations |
| Rappelling Kit | Common | 275Ç | Controlled descent |

**Multitool** — A compact folding tool covering the most common field requirements: blade, pliers, screwdrivers, wire cutters, and a handful of other implements that become essential at unpredictable moments. The baseline piece of kit that every operator carries and uses more than they expect to. Cheap enough that losing one isn't a problem; useful enough that not having one always is.

**Crowbar** — A length of hardened steel that opens doors, breaks locks, pries panels, and functions as a serviceable melee weapon when nothing else is available. The crowbar is the oldest tool in the operator's kit and remains relevant in 2099 for the same reason it was relevant in every century before: physics hasn't changed and neither have doors.

**Cutting Torch** — A compact plasma cutting tool for when a crowbar isn't sufficient — reinforced doors, locked hinges, security panels, and anything else that requires removing material rather than moving it. Takes longer than a crowbar and requires a power cell, but cuts through things a crowbar cannot. An obvious entry tool that leaves obvious evidence of use.

**Grappling Hook** — A compact pneumatic launcher and hook system for gaining vertical access to structures. Rated for operator weight plus standard gear load. The standard solution for rooftop entry, window access from below, and any situation where the ground-level approach is covered and the vertical approach isn't. Requires practice to place accurately under pressure.

**Climbing Gear** — Harness, rope, ascenders, and the supporting equipment for extended vertical operations — building exteriors, cliff faces, elevator shafts, and any environment where you need to move vertically over distance and do it reliably. More comprehensive than a grappling hook setup and slower to deploy; the choice when speed is less important than control.

**Rappelling Kit** — Harness, descender, and rope system for controlled descent from height. The exit tool for operators who went up and need to come down quickly and quietly. Faster than climbing gear for descent, quieter than a grappling hook, and essential for anyone who regularly operates above ground level.

## Transportation

Getting around NYTE City means choosing between ground and air, speed and cost, and whether you want a record of where you went.

|               |                  |                |                          |
|---------------|------------------|----------------|--------------------------|
| **Item**      | **Availability** | **Cost**       | **Notes**                |
| Grounder Taxi | Common           | 2.00Ç / minute | Ground transport, logged |
| Jumper Taxi   | Common           | 3.50Ç / minute | Air transport, visible   |

**Grounder Taxi** — Ground-based automated transport with a top speed of approximately 130 km/h. The standard way most of NYTE City moves — available on demand, metered by the minute, and fully logged by the city's transport grid. Fast enough for most purposes; slower than a Jumper when traffic is bad, which in NYTE City means most of the time.

**Jumper Taxi** — Air-based automated transport with a top speed of approximately 320 km/h, operating above street level and largely immune to ground traffic. More expensive per minute but significantly faster point-to-point. Also more visible — a Jumper arrival is harder to miss than a Grounder pulling up to the curb. Operators who need to arrive quietly take the Grounder and walk the last block.

## Clothing

What you wear tells the city something about who you are before you open your mouth. In NYTE City, that first impression matters — whether you're trying to blend into a crowd, walk into a boardroom, or survive a firefight.

|                      |                  |          |                              |
|----------------------|------------------|----------|------------------------------|
| **Item**             | **Availability** | **Cost** | **Notes**                    |
| Street Clothes       | Common           | 271Ç     | Durable everyday wear        |
| Work Uniform         | Common           | 440Ç     | Professional non-corporate   |
| Tactical             | Common           | 280Ç     | Operator underlayer          |
| Suit (Low Quality)   | Common           | 550Ç     | Entry professional wear      |
| Suit (High Quality)  | Uncommon         | 1,500Ç   | Corporate status wear        |
| Accessories (Base)   | Common           | 225Ç     | Standard jewelry and eyewear |
| Accessories (Good)   | Common           | 600Ç     | Flashy statement pieces      |
| Accessories (Lavish) | Uncommon         | 1,200Ç   | Luxury status accessories    |

**Street Clothes** — Good clothes that are durable and common in most stores. The baseline of not drawing attention — unremarkable in any neighborhood, easy to replace when they get damaged, and the right choice for anyone who needs to move through the city without signaling anything about who they are or what they do.

**Work Uniform** — Professional clothing for people whose job requires them to look put-together without being in a suit. Security guards, service industry workers, medical technicians, trade professionals — anyone who needs to project competence and employment without projecting wealth. In certain neighborhoods, looking employed is its own kind of protection.

**Tactical** — Purpose-built clothing for rough situations: abrasion-resistant, moisture-wicking, and designed to be worn under armor without bunching or compromising fit. Unremarkable when the armor comes off. The difference between an operator who's comfortable six hours into a job and one who isn't.

**Suit (Low Quality)** — A standard suit for business wear. Signals professionalism and basic investment in appearance without suggesting significant wealth. Gets you into most rooms that require a suit. Won't impress anyone looking closely at the fabric.

**Suit (High Quality)** — The ideological high fashion of the corporate oligarch. The cut, the fabric, the construction — everything signals that the person wearing it operates at a level where the price of the suit is not a consideration. Required equipment for environments where showing up in anything less closes doors permanently.

**Accessories (Base)** — Baseline quality accessories — jewelry, sunglasses, and other finishing pieces that complete an outfit without calling attention to themselves.

**Accessories (Good)** — Flashy jewelry and fashionwear that make a statement. The choice of operators who want their appearance to do social work before they open their mouth.

**Accessories (Lavish)** — Luxurious jewelry and accessories used by the wealthy. At this price point, accessories aren't finishing touches — they're the point. The rest of the outfit exists to support them.

## Food & Drink

Nobody runs well on an empty stomach. NYTE City's food economy ranges from nutritionally adequate to genuinely good, with a few luxuries for those who can afford them.

|                  |                  |          |                          |
|------------------|------------------|----------|--------------------------|
| **Item**         | **Availability** | **Cost** | **Notes**                |
| Coffee           | Common           | 11Ç      | Everywhere, always       |
| Common Bar Drink | Common           | 9Ç       | Standard pour            |
| 6 Pack           | Common           | 15Ç      | Convenience store staple |
| Fast Food Meal   | Common           | 17Ç      | Technically food         |
| Real Meat        | Uncommon         | 30Ç / lb | Luxury protein source    |
| High Class Dish  | Uncommon         | 115Ç+    | Actually food            |

**Coffee** — Typical quality beverage found all over NYTE City, in every format and at every hour. The universal constant of the city's economy. Available everywhere, consumed by everyone, and one of the few things that costs the same in the working districts as it does in the corporate towers.

**Common Bar Drink** — A standard pour at any bar in NYTE City. The kind of drink you order when you need somewhere to sit and something in your hand, not because you're particularly interested in the drink.

**6 Pack** — Average quality beer or alcohol from any convenience store. The economy option for unwinding at the end of a job. Nobody's ordering this for the taste.

**Fast Food Meal** — A common combination meal from any of the hundreds of automated kiosks and chain outlets that line NYTE City's commercial corridors. It technically meets a narrow definition of nutritional requirements. Nobody eats it because it's good; they eat it because it's there and it takes forty-five seconds to obtain.

**Real Meat** — An uncommon food source in a city where soy-based supplements dominate the food supply chain. Real animal protein — not processed soy — is a modest luxury that signals either access to better supply chains or the willingness to spend significantly more on a meal. Sold by the pound at specialty grocers and upmarket restaurants.

**High Class Dish** — Food prepared at a high-quality restaurant by actual people using actual ingredients. More expensive than fast food in every measurable way and better in every measurable way. One of the small pleasures available in a city that isn't known for them.

## Lodging

A place to sleep, clean up, and not be found. NYTE City offers options at every price point and every level of discretion — from the coffin box that fits a body and not much else to the hotel room that pretends the city outside doesn't exist.

|                 |                  |              |                             |
|-----------------|------------------|--------------|-----------------------------|
| **Item**        | **Availability** | **Cost**     | **Notes**                   |
| Coffin Box      | Common           | 85Ç / month  | Minimum viable living       |
| ConAp           | Common           | 650Ç / month | Functional budget apartment |
| Motel (Cheap)   | Common           | 65Ç / night  | No questions asked          |
| Motel (Average) | Common           | 85Ç / night  | Standard amenities          |
| Hotel (Cheap)   | Common           | 120Ç / night | Minor luxuries              |
| Hotel (Average) | Uncommon         | 350Ç / night | Mid-tier comfort            |

**Coffin Box** — A low-standard living space often packed into large residential buildings alongside dozens or hundreds of others. A bed, a storage unit, a screen, and enough room to stand up in. The minimum viable living arrangement in NYTE City — chosen by those who have no other option and by operators who need a temporary address in a specific district and nothing more.

**ConAp** — Convenience Apartment: cheap but functional monthly housing that sits between a coffin box and a real apartment. A kitchen, a bathroom, a sleeping area, and enough space to not feel like you're living in a locker. The default long-term housing for Working class NYTE City residents who can't afford better and refuse to live in a coffin box.

**Motel (Cheap)** — A basic facility with a shower, a bed, and a holo-V setup. Rents by the night and doesn't ask questions, which is the primary feature for a significant portion of its clientele. The lock works. Nobody who works the desk remembers anyone's face.

**Motel (Average)** — A standard room with decent amenities, functional climate control, and a level of cleanliness that doesn't require inspection before use. More expensive than the cheap option and reliably has working hot water. Unremarkable in the way that's actually useful.

**Hotel (Cheap)** — A more comfortable room with minor luxuries — better linens, actual room service, a lobby that doesn't smell like the street outside. The step up from a motel for operators who need to meet clients in a space that communicates a minimum level of professionalism.

**Hotel (Average)** — A mid-priced space with room service, minor luxury services, and the kind of anonymity that comes with professional front desk staff trained not to notice things. The choice of corporate travelers and operators who need a clean, comfortable base of operations without drawing attention.

# Vehicles, Powered Armor & Mech Suits

A Grounder Taxi gets you across the city. A Sentinel gets you across it safely. A Vanguard Warden mech gets you across it while everything in the way reconsiders its position. Vehicles in NYTE City exist on a spectrum from civilian transport to mobile weapons platforms, and the rules that govern them scale accordingly.

This chapter covers three categories: **Vehicles** (Grounders and Jumpers), **Powered Armor** (Iron Man end of the spectrum — worn, amplifying), and **Mech Suits** (D.VA end — piloted, independent). All three use the same core framework. What changes is the scale.

### How Vehicles Work

#### The Core Principle: Disable, Don't Kill

Vehicles, powered armor, and mech suits are not targets you kill — they are targets you *disable*. The goal in vehicle combat is to destroy systems, not pilots. A Grounder with a destroyed drivetrain is a stationary obstacle. A mech with disabled legs is a turret. A powered armor suit with a locked-up servo system is a very expensive coffin until the wearer extracts.

Standard weapons can damage vehicles, but meaningful progress requires either sustained fire over many rounds or weapons with the **Massive** damage category. A pistol can scratch a Sentinel's paint. It will not stop one. Weapons with the **Anti-Materiel**, **Siege**, or **Blast** tags deal full damage to vehicles. Everything else deals reduced effect — at the GM's discretion, standard weapons may deal chip damage or no meaningful damage at all against heavily armored vehicles.

#### Vehicle Stats

**PROT** — Die roll that soaks incoming damage from any source. Rolled every time the vehicle takes a hit, same as personal armor. Vehicle PROT dice are larger than personal armor — a civilian Grounder rolls 1d6, a military mech rolls 1d12.

**RES** — Flat damage reduction against Kinetic attacks (Ballistic, Blade, Blunt). Represents the structural density of the vehicle's armor. Much higher than personal armor values — a vehicle's RES reflects that it was built to absorb sustained fire, not individual shots.

**INT (Integrity)** — The vehicle's structural hit point pool. Represents overall hull integrity and system health. When INT reaches zero the vehicle is **Wrecked** — it cannot move or fight, though the pilot/occupants may survive depending on circumstances. INT is repaired at a garage or maintenance facility; field repairs restore limited INT but do not restore disabled systems.

**Systems** — Discrete subsystems that can be targeted and disabled independently of overall INT. Standard systems include:

- **Propulsion** — Movement and speed. Disabled: vehicle cannot move.

- **Weapons** — Mounted weapon systems. Disabled: vehicle cannot fire mounted weapons.

- **Sensors/Electronics** — HUD, targeting, communications. Disabled: lose all electronic bonuses.

- **Life Support** — Pilot protection and environmental systems. Only relevant when INT reaches 0 or a System Failure result affects it directly.

#### INTEGRITY CHECKS

Certain events trigger an Integrity Check — a percentile roll against the vehicle's current Integrity percentage. If the check fails, roll on the System Failure table.

Integrity Checks are triggered by:

- Taking a hit from a **Massive** damage weapon

- Taking a hit from an **EMP** source (grenade, rifle, or beam)

- Accumulating damage that reduces INT by 25% or more in a single round

- A called shot targeting a specific system (GM discretion)

The Integrity Check percentage starts at the vehicle's base Integrity rating and decreases as INT is lost. A vehicle at 50% INT has a 50% chance of passing its Integrity Check. A vehicle at 10% INT is barely holding together.

#### SYSTEM FAILURE TABLE

Roll 1d100 when an Integrity Check fails. Results apply to Powered Armor and Mech Suits alike — the fiction determines whether "right arm disabled" means a powered gauntlet or a mech appendage. The consequence is the same.

|  |  |
|----|----|
| **Roll** | **Result** |
| 01–30 | **No Internal Damage.** The system holds. You got lucky. |
| 31–40 | **Temporary System Outage.** General malfunction imposes −2 on all combat actions. Systems recover in 1d4 rounds. |
| 41–50 | **Power Grid Fluctuation.** Melee/physical damage bonuses suffer −5. Lifting heavy objects increases difficulty by +3. Power redistributes in 1d4 rounds, clearing both penalties. |
| 51–60 | **Limb Disabled.** A limb loses function from direct hit or power failure. If the hit targeted a specific limb, that limb is disabled. Otherwise roll 1d4: Right Arm (1), Left Arm (2), Right Leg (3), Left Leg (4). A disabled leg halves movement speed. Requires repair to restore. |
| 61–70 | **Internal Feedback Malfunction.** A power surge damages the pilot/wearer directly. Take 1d6 Energy damage, bypassing personal armor. |
| 71–75 | **Communications Destroyed.** No tight-beam or radio communications. Verbal communication requires opening the faceplate or cockpit. Nearly impossible to hear the pilot otherwise. |
| 76–80 | **System Lockup.** All servos and joints lock. The vehicle or suit cannot move at all. System reset takes 1d6 rounds. Extraction is impossible until the lockup clears. |
| 81–85 | **HUD Failure.** All HUD data goes dark: SMART weapon bonuses lost, NAV points invisible, spectrum vision and night vision offline, onboard weapons cannot be fired, motion detection and targeting data unavailable. The visor or cockpit display is now just transparent. |
| 86–90 | **General Malfunction.** Roll 1d6: Onboard weapons fire at random targets (1) / Mobility systems fire at irregular intervals for 1 round (2) / System restarts, disabling the suit or vehicle for 1d4 rounds (3) / HUD drops to half reliability for 10 rounds, −2 on all combat checks (4) / Emergency extraction triggers automatically, ejecting the pilot (5) / Minor short circuit fills the cockpit or visor with smoke, −1 to all combat checks for 3 rounds or until cleared (6). |
| 91–93 | **Power Rupture.** The vehicle emits charged particles or an elevated EMF signature, making it trivially detectable by enemy sensors. All stealth checks against sensor-equipped opponents automatically fail until repaired. |
| 94–95 | **IFF Failure.** Friend-or-foe identification locks out combat functionality. Onboard weapons are disabled. No accuracy bonuses when friendlies are in combat proximity or targets are in cover. Requires repair. |
| 96–99 | **Critical System Failure.** HUD fully offline. The vehicle or suit cannot move without extreme effort. Emergency systems engage, allowing pilot extraction without penalty — unless the suit's structural integrity has also been compromised, in which case extraction imposes a −3 penalty on relevant checks. |
| 00 | **Double Whammy.** Roll twice on this table. If 00 appears again, reroll until a different result appears — it does not stack. |

### Pilot Skill

All vehicles, powered armor, and mech suits are governed by the **Pilot** skill. The **Wheeler** professional archetype gains a bonus to all Pilot checks regardless of vehicle type — a Wheeler who can drive a Grounder can adapt to a Jumper or a mech faster than a standard operator.

Powered Armor is a special case. Because it amplifies the pilot's own body rather than replacing their movement, pilots use their personal combat skills (Melee, Rifles, Handguns, etc.) while inside powered armor — the suit enhances those skills rather than substituting for them. The Pilot skill governs getting into, out of, and operating the suit's systems. Combat uses the pilot's own skill ranks, modified by the suit's enhancement bonuses.

Mech Suits operate differently. The pilot interfaces through the suit's VI and operating system rather than moving their own body. Pilot skill governs mech movement, targeting, and system management. Personal combat skills do not apply inside a mech cockpit.

### EMP and Vehicles

EMP damage — from grenades, the Nullifier, or other sources — automatically triggers an Integrity Check regardless of damage dealt. Vehicles with **EMP Shielding** installed gain a bonus to this check. Vehicles without shielding are particularly vulnerable to EMP tactics, which is why prepared operators carry the Blackout grenade and why the Nullifier is one of the most tactically interesting weapons in the chapter.

A vehicle reduced to 0 INT by EMP is not destroyed — it is simply offline. Structural damage is minimal; systems are fried. This is the preferred outcome for operators who want the vehicle intact (for extraction, capture, or salvage) rather than burning.

### Wrecked vs Destroyed

A vehicle at 0 INT is **Wrecked** — nonfunctional, but potentially repairable. The pilot and occupants may survive depending on how the INT was depleted and whether Life Support failed.

A vehicle that takes **Massive** damage beyond 0 INT, or that suffers a catastrophic result at 0 INT, is **Destroyed** — structurally compromised beyond repair. Pilot survival at this point is at the GM's discretion and is not guaranteed.

The distinction matters for salvage, for extraction, and for the question of whether the enemy's mech can be repaired and turned against them.

## Vehicles

Getting around NYTE City is its own discipline. The city moves — on the ground through a grid of elevated highways, surface streets, and underground corridors, and in the air through stacked traffic lanes that run between buildings at a dozen different altitudes. A character without reliable transport is a character who arrives late, leaves slow, and gets caught in the wrong place when things go wrong.

Vehicles in Shadows fall into two categories: **Grounders** (wheeled or hover-based surface transport) and **Jumpers** (aerial vehicles that navigate the city's vertical traffic grid). Both are available for purchase, hire, or acquisition by other means. Some are everyday civilian hardware. Some are built for war. A few were built by someone's cousin in a garage and probably shouldn't be trusted at highway speeds.

### Vehicle Stats at a Glance

**PROT** — Die roll on every hit, soaks damage of any type. Roll when the vehicle takes fire.

**RES** — Flat kinetic damage reduction. Applied after PROT. Much higher than personal armor — vehicles are built to absorb sustained fire.

**INT** — Integrity pool. Functions as hit points for vehicles — what gets through PROT and RES comes off INT. At 0, the vehicle is Wrecked and cannot move or fight. Larger vehicles have larger INT pools; a Crotchrocket goes down faster than an Enigma Striker XL, which goes down faster than a Punknaught.

**Speed** — Top operational speed under normal conditions. Combat maneuvers reduce effective speed at GM discretion.

**Seats** — Maximum occupant capacity including pilot.

**Mods** — Available modification slots for upgrades and armor kits.

**Availability / Cost** — Same framework as weapons and armor. Street vehicles and civilian models are Common; military-grade hardware is Rare or Exotic.

### Grounders

Grounders are the surface vehicles of NYTE City — two-wheeled and four-wheeled, wheeled and hover-based, civilian commuters and armored carriers. The city's ground grid is the domain of daily life: taxis and delivery drones and corporate convoys and gangs who've claimed specific routes as territory. A Grounder is the most common vehicle most characters will ever need, and the range runs from something a teenager cobbled together from scavenged parts to something Enigma Defense sells to governments.

|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| **Vehicle** | **Seats** | **PROT** | **RES** | **INT** | **Speed** | **Mods** | **Availability** | **Cost** |
| Crotchrocket | 2 | 1d4 | 2 | 50 | 120 km/h | 1 | Common | 2,000Ç |
| Solaris Stellar | 4 | 1d6 | 4 | 100 | 90 km/h | 2 | Common | 5,000Ç |
| Arcadian G7 | 6 | 1d8 | 6 | 150 | 100 km/h | 3 | Common | 8,000Ç |
| Arcadian Infinity Executive | 4 | 1d8 | 8 | 130 | 110 km/h | 6 | Uncommon | 12,000Ç |
| Enigma Striker XL | 8 | 1d10 | 10 | 200 | 80 km/h | 4 | Uncommon | 15,000Ç |
| Punknaught | 20 | 1d10 | 8 | 300 | 70 km/h | 6 | — | — |

**Crotchrocket** — Not a model name — a category. A Crotchrocket is whatever two-wheeled vehicle someone put together from scavenged e-bike components, salvaged battery packs, and enough structural confidence to get it moving at speed. No two are quite the same. The stat block represents the average of what these things tend to be, which varies considerably depending on who built it and what they had available. Fast, loud, and requires more maintenance than the owner usually admits. Stats represent a typical example — actual capabilities vary by build and builder.

**Solaris Stellar** — The default vehicle of NYTE City's streets. Solaris built the Stellar for families and practical commuters, and the city's taxi services adopted it as their standard platform — when a PC hails a grounder cab, a Stellar pulls up. It seats four comfortably, handles the city grid without complaint, and comes in enough color options to be completely forgettable in traffic. The kind of vehicle that blends into every neighborhood simultaneously, which makes it quietly popular with operators who need transport that doesn't draw attention and with taxi operators who need a vehicle that runs all day without complaint.

**Arcadian G7** — Arcadian's mid-range entry is the default corporate transport — the vehicle that pulls up to the lobby when a mid-level executive needs a ride, and the vehicle that tails that executive when someone needs to know where they're going. Six seats, solid armor, driver-assist systems that can handle most of the city grid on automation. Not flashy. Built to be depended on.

**Arcadian Infinity Executive** — Autonomous driving, advanced safety architecture, and an interior designed around the premise that the passenger's time is worth more than the driver's attention. The Infinity Executive is what upper management rides when they want to work during the commute rather than navigate it. The six modification slots reflect a chassis that was designed from the beginning to accept premium upgrades. The vehicle is Common enough that nobody looks twice — which is its own kind of luxury.

**Enigma Striker XL** — Enigma Defense's standard armored transport for law enforcement and private security contracts. Seats eight operatives in full kit, carries enough armor to shrug off most small arms fire, and comes with weapon mount pre-points that Enigma will sell you the weapons for separately. Not subtle — it looks exactly like what it is. Which is, for many of its operators, precisely the point.

**Punknaught** — Nobody manufactured a Punknaught. Someone built the first one, and then other people looked at it and thought that was a reasonable thing to do. The Punknaught is a heavy carrier constructed from scavenged vehicle platforms, mismatched armor plating, jury-rigged weapon mounts, and structural optimism. It carries up to twenty people through environments that would stop anything more refined. No two are identical. The crew names theirs. Cost and availability are listed as — because Punknaughts aren't purchased — they're built, stolen, inherited, or won. Stats represent a typical example — actual capabilities vary considerably by build and by the state the previous owner left it in.

### Jumpers

NYTE City moves most of its population through an extensive commuter rail network that handles the volume no road or air system could sustain. Personal vehicles fill the gaps — the last mile, the off-grid errand, the job that can't go through a monitored transit system. Jumpers operate in this space, navigating the city's vertical airspace between buildings rather than across the country. Long-distance travel happens via mass transit; Jumpers go building to building, rooftop to rooftop, district to district.

The airspace above the NY Metro Core is organized into three primary bands — Low, Mid, and Upper — with a restricted fourth band reserved for emergency services and authorized military traffic. Jumpers weave between towers within these designated lanes, visible to each other and to the city's traffic management systems at all times. The lanes aren't congested to the point of gridlock; NYTE City's urban planning accounted for aerial density in ways its ground planners didn't. But they are monitored, and a Jumper operating outside designated lanes is immediately flagged.

Jumpers park on rooftop pads, in building bays, and on designated street-level platforms. They don't require runways. Some carry onboard weapon systems — the Thunderbolt most visibly — but aerial combat between Jumpers is an unusual edge case. The practical use of Jumper weapons is ground suppression: covering an extraction, clearing a landing zone, keeping heads down while someone reaches the roof. Two Jumpers shooting at each other over a NYTE City tower block is a scene that draws attention from every direction simultaneously, which is usually reason enough not to start it.

| **Vehicle** | **Seats** | **PROT** | **RES** | **INT** | **Speed** | **Mods** | **Availability** | **Cost** |
| Hyperion Eclipse | 2 | 1d4 | 2 | 70 | 250 km/h | 1 | Common | 10,000Ç |
| Atlas SkyHawk L2 | 4 | 1d6 | 4 | 120 | 200 km/h | 2 | Common | 20,000Ç |
| Arcadian Aero Executive | 6 | 1d8 | 6 | 180 | 220 km/h | 3 | Uncommon | 35,000Ç |
| Atlas Thunderbolt | 6 | 1d10 | 10 | 250 | 180 km/h | 5 | Rare | 50,000Ç |

**Hyperion Eclipse** — A compact two-seat personal Jumper built for speed and agility in urban airspace. The Eclipse is what you buy when you've decided that ground traffic is someone else's problem — sleek, fast, and maneuverable enough to navigate the tighter corridors of the city's mid-altitude grid. Minimal armor reflects that the Eclipse was designed around not being hit rather than absorbing hits. Popular with couriers, fixers, and anyone whose time is valuable enough to justify the price difference over a Grounder taxi.

**Atlas SkyHawk L2** — Atlas Aerospace's standard civilian Jumper: mid-sized, four-seat, designed for both passenger and cargo configurations. The SkyHawk L2 is the workhorse of NYTE City's air traffic — common enough that seeing one overhead registers as background noise rather than an event. Modular interior makes it adaptable to whatever the operator needs it for. A patron who sends a SkyHawk to pick the party up is sending a professional message. A patron who sends an Arcadian Aero is sending a different one.

**Arcadian Aero Executive** — The aerial equivalent of the Infinity Executive: autonomous-capable, premium interior, and an exterior that signals that whoever is inside does not ride in SkyHawks. The Aero Executive descends to private rooftop pads, not public landing zones. It is the vehicle that corporate security rides when escorting someone worth protecting, and the vehicle that observers note when it lands somewhere it shouldn't. Three mod slots make it upgradeable for operators who need the status of civilian luxury and the capability of something more serious.

**Atlas Thunderbolt** — The Atlas Thunderbolt was designed for tactical operations, and it looks like it. Heavy armor for a Jumper, multiple weapon mount points, advanced sensor and communications systems, and enough interior space for six operators in full kit. It is not a subtle vehicle — a Thunderbolt descending on a location announces itself. That announcement is, for many of its operators, the message they want to send. Rare availability reflects that Atlas sells the Thunderbolt to vetted clients through a process that the company describes as rigorous and everyone else describes as expensive.

## Vehicle Armor Kits

Vehicle armor kits are aftermarket upgrades applied to Grounder and Jumper chassis, increasing their protective capability beyond factory specification. Each kit occupies one or more mod slots and requires professional installation — a garage with the right equipment, not a field repair kit and an optimistic attitude.

Kits are rated Light, Medium, or Heavy and cover either **Panels** (body armor — doors, hood, chassis) or **Windows** (transparent ballistic glazing — windshield and side glass). Most operators prioritize panel coverage; window upgrades matter most for operators who expect to be shot at from the front while moving.

Vehicle armor kits do not stack INT pools — they increase RES values rather than adding to the integrity pool. The chassis's structural integrity is determined by its base INT.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| **Kit** | **Manufacturer** | **Type** | **RES Bonus** | **Coverage** | **Availability** | **Notes** |
| Reinforcement | Various | Light | +10 | Panels | Common | Does not affect top speed |
| Roadrunner Armor Kit | Various | Light | +14 | Panels | Common | Grounders only |
| Shinsei Razercat Kit | Shinsei Defense | Light | +18 | Panels | Uncommon | Jumper compatible |
| Shinsei Interceptor Package | Shinsei Defense | Light | +20 | Panels + Windows | Uncommon | Jumper optimized |
| Shinsei Shadow Wrap | Shinsei Defense | Light | +16 | Panels | Rare | E-Chrome integrated, stealth |
| DarkSun K1 Kit | DarkSun | Medium | +26 | Panels | Uncommon | Jumper compatible |
| Bullet Proofing | Various | Medium | +27 | Windows | Uncommon | Transparent ballistic glazing |
| Thunder Gunner Kit | Various | Heavy | +33 | Panels | Rare | Large Grounders only |
| Irongate Hauler Reinforcements | Irongate Heavy | Heavy | +38 | Panels | Rare | Heavy Grounders only |
| Irongate Breach Plating | Irongate Heavy | Heavy | +35 | Front panels | Rare | Ramming optimized |
| Blast Shield | Various | Heavy | +40 | Windows | Rare | Retractable option available |
| Irongate Fortress Kit | Irongate Heavy | Heavy | +45 | Full body | Exotic | Lockdown Mode capable |

**Reinforcement** — A general application of composite armor plating to all major vehicle panels. Light enough that it doesn't affect the vehicle's performance or top speed, which makes it the most popular baseline upgrade for operators who want some protection without announcing that they're expecting trouble. Available for any vehicle. Does not require specialist installation beyond a competent garage.

**Roadrunner Armor Kit** — A full-body light armor upgrade common among street gangs and low-level mercenaries who need more protection than stock but can't afford anything heavier. The material is heavier than the Shinsei Defense alternative and cannot be applied to Jumpers without power output modifications that aren't worth the cost. For Grounders, it's a straightforward and effective upgrade at a price point that reflects its target market.

**Shinsei Razercat Kit** — Shinsei Defense's composite armor technology achieves something most light kits don't: genuine durability at genuinely low weight. The Razercat Kit is compatible with both Grounders and Jumpers — light enough that it doesn't compromise a Jumper's lift capacity or a Grounder's performance. Favored across the professional spectrum from corporate security to independent operators who can't afford the weight penalty of heavier alternatives.

**DarkSun K1 Kit** — DarkSun's vehicle armor entry applies the same composite durability philosophy as their personal armor line. The K1 handles larger AVs and Grounders without issue and sits at a price point that makes it accessible to mid-tier operators. Sleek enough that it doesn't visually transform whatever it's applied to into something that looks combat-ready, which has its own tactical value.

**Bullet Proofing** — Ballistic-resistant transparent material applied to vehicle windows, making it significantly harder to put a round through the glass and into whoever is sitting behind it. Specific application — windows only — but addresses a genuine vulnerability that panel armor doesn't cover. Most professional operators install both panel and window upgrades rather than choosing between them.

**Thunder Gunner Kit** — Heavy composite plating designed for large Grounders, APCs, and military dropships. The Thunder Gunner Kit is the step up to serious protection — the kind of armor that changes the calculus of what weapons are required to meaningfully threaten the vehicle. Requires a large vehicle chassis to apply; attempting to install it on a civilian sedan produces a vehicle that cannot move under its own weight.

**Irongate Hauler Reinforcements** — The heaviest panel armor available for ground vehicles — effectively tank-grade protection applied to a Grounder chassis. Full-body application on heavier vehicles turns them into something capable of taking sustained heavy weapons fire. No Jumper can carry this weight regardless of power output modifications. The name reflects its origin in heavy cargo transport that needed to be able to drive through active combat zones.

**Blast Shield** — A rigid, high-strength shield covering vulnerable points on the vehicle — primarily glass surfaces and exposed mechanical components. Available in permanent and retractable configurations. The permanent installation includes a digital mask display that maintains occupant visibility through opaque shielding; the retractable version deploys on demand and allows normal visibility when not in use. The heaviest window protection available and the only kit rated for blast-level protection rather than ballistic.

**Shinsei Interceptor Package** — Shinsei's combined solution for operators who want full protection in a single installation: Razercat-grade panel composite plus ballistic window glazing in one package, weight-optimized for Jumper compatibility. The Interceptor is what Atlas Aerospace recommends for SkyHawk operators working in contested airspace — everything covered, nothing added to the weight envelope that wasn't planned for.

**Shinsei Shadow Wrap** — Shinsei Defense's stealth-adjacent offering: light composite panels with E-Chrome coating integrated at manufacture rather than applied afterward. The Shadow Wrap responds to the vehicle's environment, shifting surface appearance for reduced visual signature. Doesn't make the vehicle invisible — makes it harder to track visually in motion and harder to distinguish from background at distance. Popular with operators who do work they'd prefer wasn't documented.

**Irongate Breach Plating** — Front-facing reinforced plating specifically engineered for vehicles that are going to make contact with things at speed. Irongate didn't design the Breach Plating for ramming, but their engineers understood exactly what operators were going to do with it and built accordingly. Covers the front panels and bumper structure. The vehicle hits harder than it would unarmored, and the vehicle survives the experience better than the thing it hit.

**Irongate Fortress Kit** — The full Irongate treatment: maximum-weight composite plating across every panel, blast-rated window glazing, reinforced door seals, and automated **Lockdown Mode**. When Lockdown is engaged, all external panels lock to full-closed, blast shields deploy over every window, and the vehicle becomes essentially impenetrable to anything below Siege or Massive damage category weapons. The tradeoff is total: occupants cannot see out through conventional means (sensor systems required), speed drops to roughly half, and the vehicle is committed to its current direction until Lockdown disengages. What it is in Lockdown Mode is a rolling bunker — blind, slow, and capable of absorbing a sustained firefight that would destroy anything else on this list. Only heavy Grounders can carry the Fortress Kit's weight. No Jumper can. The only things that reliably threaten a Fortress Kit vehicle in Lockdown are weapons that were designed to fight buildings, not people.

# Powered Armor

Powered armor is not a vehicle. It is worn — the operator moves, the suit amplifies. The distinction matters: a powered armor operator fights with their own skills, their own training, and their own instincts. The suit makes them faster, stronger, and harder to kill. It does not replace them.

What powered armor does is change the scale of what a person can do. An operator in a Renzo X1 moves at three times normal speed, hits with six times the effective strength, and carries combat systems that would require a vehicle in any other context. They are still a person. They are a person who has become a significant tactical problem.

Powered armor operators use their personal combat skills — Melee, Rifles, Handguns, Martial Arts — enhanced by the suit's physical bonuses. Enhanced mobility means moving faster, jumping farther, and traversing terrain that would stop an unarmored operator — not necessarily leaving the ground to soar through the sky. At least, not easily.

All powered armor uses the Integrity Check and System Failure table defined in the core vehicle rules. At the GM's discretion, called shots targeting specific suit components may trigger Integrity Checks regardless of damage dealt.

### Powered Armor Stats

**PROT** — Die roll on every hit, same as personal armor but scaled up to vehicle tier.

**RES** — Flat kinetic damage reduction. Uses the same material-based values as personal armor — the suit's construction determines its resistance profile.

**INT** — Integrity pool. Tracks suit structural health. At 0 the suit is non-functional; the operator is effectively unarmored and must extract or be extracted.

**Physical Enhancements** — Stat bonuses applied to the operator while the suit is powered and functional. Lost when the suit reaches 0 INT or suffers relevant System Failure results.

**Software Enhancements** — Skill bonuses and VI-assisted capabilities built into the suit's operating system. Also lost on HUD failure or critical system failure results.

**Standard Features** — Built-in hardware that comes with the suit at purchase.

**Combat System Package** — The HUD and sensor suite installed in the helmet. Class I through IV, defined in the Combat System Packages section.

### Darksun Power Sleeves

- *Partial Coverage — Arms and Hands*

- *Helmet: Class III Combat System Package*

A set of strength-enhancing armored sleeves that connect across the back to support heavy lifting and close-quarters combat. Originally developed for industrial and emergency applications, the Power Sleeves have found their market among operators who want enhanced physical capability without committing to a full suit. Simple enough technologically that system failure risks are minimal — fewer systems means fewer things to go wrong. The DS Power Sleeves couple naturally with armored vests or partial suits for operators who want to build their own protection profile rather than buy into a complete solution.

- Strength Enhancement: +4 to all BOD based Skill checks and damage

Neurodyne Industries built the Glimmer Man around their neurological research into brainwave pattern recognition, and the ThirdEye OS shows it — the suit reacts as fast as the wearer can think, treating the operator's neural signals as direct input rather than translating physical movement. The armor is durable, uses Tri-Weave lining to keep the operator comfortable during extended wear, and deploys via lockplate technology that allows extraction without assistance. The angular design with its medieval influence and full heavy visor reads as menacing before the operator has moved a muscle. The chest piece's ridged V-profile is specifically engineered to deflect projectiles from the face.

### Shinsei Renzo X1

- *Full Body Coverage — Modular Configuration*

- *Helmet: Class IV Combat System Package*

- *Availability: Exotic (By Invitation)*

The Renzo X1 is not purchased off a shelf. It is configured — a conversation between the client and Shinsei's design team that begins with the base chassis and ends with a suit built specifically for the operator who will wear it. The price listed is the entry point: the platform, the lockplate system, the angular composite plating with its Japanese design influence, and the Class IV helmet that represents the most sophisticated combat systems package in the powered armor market. What that price becomes after configuration depends entirely on what the client needs.

The modular architecture is the point. Physical enhancement packages, software overlays, weapon mounts, stealth integration, additional sensor systems — each is a separate specification decision, and Shinsei's engineers will spend considerable time ensuring each addition works with the others. An operator who specs a Renzo X1 for close-quarters melee gets a different suit than one who specs it for long-range precision work, and both are different from the suit Shinsei builds for someone who primarily needs the strength enhancement for industrial applications. The chassis handles all of it. The final invoice reflects the choices.

Exotic availability means Shinsei chooses its clients as much as its clients choose Shinsei. The invitation process is opaque and the criteria are not published. What is known is that certain operators have Renzo X1 suits, which tells the people who know what they're looking at something significant about those operators.

#### Base Physical Enhancements (included):

- Enhanced Reflexes: +3 to REF based Skill Checks

- Enhanced Mobility: Run, Sprint, Jump ×3

- Enhanced Strength: +6 to all BOD based Skill Checks and hand-to-hand damage

*Additional configuration options available at Shinsei's discretion. Base cost reflects unmodified chassis only.*

# Mech Suits

A mech suit is not powered armor. Powered armor is worn — the operator moves and the suit amplifies. A mech suit is piloted — the operator sits inside it, interfaces through its operating system, and directs a machine that moves independently of their body. The distinction matters in combat, in capability, and in what skills govern the machine.

Mech suit operators use the **Pilot** skill for all movement, targeting, and system management. Personal combat skills do not apply inside a mech cockpit. What applies is the operator's ability to direct a several-ton bipedal weapons platform through an urban environment without losing it — and to do so effectively when the environment is shooting back.

Mechs are not common. They are not personal purchases for most operators. They are faction assets, corporate property, government hardware, and occasionally the result of someone with enough money, connections, and ambition deciding they needed one. Encountering a mech in NYTE City is an event. Piloting one is a statement about who the crew is working for, or what they just did to acquire it.

All mech suits use the Integrity Check and System Failure table from the core vehicle rules. Mechs are generally targets you disable, not targets you kill — the pilot inside a functional mech is protected by the machine around them. At 0 INT the mech is **Wrecked**; the pilot is alive unless a System Failure result or Massive Damage says otherwise.

## Mech Suit Operation Notes

**Getting In and Out** — Mech suits require time to board and extract. Combat boarding under fire is a Pilot skill check. Emergency extraction on a Wrecked mech uses the System Failure table results for guidance.

**Maintenance** — Mechs require professional maintenance facilities. Field repairs restore limited INT but do not restore disabled systems. A Wrecked mech requires a fully equipped garage or military maintenance bay to return to service.

**Ammunition** — Belt-fed weapons on mechs carry substantial ammunition loads — treat as effectively unlimited for standard encounters, with resupply required between major operations. Power cell weapons carry the same capacity as their personal weapon equivalents and must be replaced when depleted.

**Urban Operation** — Mechs in NYTE City's urban environment are conspicuous. A combat mech moving through a residential district creates immediate response from city systems, law enforcement, and anyone in the area with enough sense to get clear. The Phantom's stealth systems reduce but do not eliminate this signature. The Colossus doesn’t even try.

## Mech Weapon Mounts

Mech suits carry weapons through dedicated mount systems rather than handheld operation. Mount size determines what weapons the chassis can support.

**Light Mount** — Compatible with any Heavy or Beam weapon from the personal weapons chapter. Belt-fed or power cell only; no weapons requiring manual reload. Standard arm-mounted configuration.

**Heavy Mount** — Vehicle-scale weapons significantly beyond personal heavy weapons. The Ironwall HMG operates as a Light Mount weapon on a mech chassis. Heavy Mount weapons are purpose-built for mech platforms.

**Siege Mount** — The largest and most destructive class. Weapons at this scale are the reason mechs exist in combat contexts. Siege Mount weapons are not available through standard channels — they come with the chassis contract or not at all.

**Tool Mount** — Non-weapon industrial equipment: Loader Jaws, Cutting Torch, Crane Arm. Can be used as improvised weapons in extremis. Not designed for combat; effective in combat nonetheless.

**Civic Mount** — Non-lethal crowd control systems: Sonic Dispersal Array, Water Cannon, Tear Gas Launchers, Restraint Net Launcher, Crowd Barrier Arms, Riot Shield Panel. Designed for crowd management rather than combat. "Non-lethal" at mech scale is a policy designation, not a physical guarantee.

*Mechs do not use weapons requiring manual reload. All mech weapons are belt-fed or power cell. The operator manages ammunition through the HUD system, not by physically reloading.*
